title: Screen in Screen
narrative: A picture of a picture changes ownership. The person on the inner screen is already framed by someone else: a director, a hacker, a parent, a god.
We watch the watcher, or we become them if the interface takes over the outer frame. It is the wrong tool when the inner screen is an unreadable glow.
If text, faces, or timing cannot be parsed, you have set dressing. Desktop films live or die on exact writing and cursor behavior.
This is not split screen. Split screen is a graphic of two presents.
Screen-in-screen is a nested world with a power relation.
how: Design a real timeline and a legible inner frame. Photograph or generate the inner picture as an asset, then place it in a monitor with correct perspective, refresh, and reflections.
Do not ask a generator to invent stable UI and accurate text in one pass if the words matter. Prompt: Screen-in-screen of [Subject], a monitor, phone, or cinema inside the cinema, nested looking.
when: Use it when looking is already mediated: security, live TV, a search on a laptop, a projectionist, a god's control room. Do not add a TV that plays nothing relevant.
vs: Frame within Frame is usually architecture. Screen-in-screen is a display with its own image.
Split Screen tiles simultaneous presents without one being a device in the other. Windows stacks architectural panes of lives.
Voyeur may watch a screen, but voyeur is the concealment ethic. Reflections can stack a face on a dark monitor, a hybrid.
examples_film: The Truman Show makes the world a production watched on screens. Videodrome infects the watcher through the tube.
Searching and Unfriended run investigation and terror through interfaces whose text and timing are the coverage. Sherlock Jr.
lets a projectionist enter the inner picture. Grammar of nested looking, not a wallpaper of monitors.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a blurry TV set, or a fake Split Screen . The tell is unreadable text, melting UI, or two images tiled with no device.
The fix is to treat the inner picture as a designed insert with real words and a physically plausible monitor.

faq.q: What is screen in screen in film?
faq.a: A display inside the shot carries its own picture: monitor, phone, cinema screen. Someone is watching a picture of someone. The inner crop, delay, and artifacts are part of the grammar.

faq.q: Screen in Screen vs Split Screen
faq.a: Split screen tiles two or more presents as a graphic. Screen-in-screen puts one picture inside a device in the other. Power and mediation differ. A control-room wall of monitors is nested looking. A graphic half-and-half of two callers is split screen unless those halves are phones in a room.

faq.q: When should I use screen in screen?
faq.a: Use it when looking is already a broadcast, a search, a tape, or a show: surveillance, desktop investigation, a film within the film. Do not add a glowing panel with no content.

faq.q: How do I prompt screen in screen for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name device and inner content. Example: Screen-in-screen of [Subject], a monitor, phone, or cinema inside the cinema, nested looking. For UI stories, render text deterministically. Do not generate the whole interface as unstable video if words must be exact.

title: Short Siding
narrative: Deny the character air and the scene tightens without a closer lens. An interrogator, a liar, a person who has just seen the worst thing: they look into almost nothing.
The leftover field behind them is wasted country they cannot use. It is the wrong tool for ordinary coverage.
Do it by accident and the shot feels like a student pan. Do it on every close-up and the trap stops meaning.
Short siding is not the same as a big empty wall. If they look into a vast field, you have negative space in the look.
Short siding specifically starves the look.
how: Put the eyes close to the edge they face. Leave the larger field behind the skull.
A profile or strong three-quarter makes the crush obvious. You can still use a 50mm or 75mm.
The crop does the violence, not a wider lens. Do not correct it in the pan.
Prompt: Short-sided framing of [Subject], look space crushed, the face near the frame edge they look toward, trapped or urgent.
when: Use it for interrogation, guilt, panic, and any beat where the next thing should feel unreachable. Do not use it as default portrait grammar.
vs: Lead Room is the polite reverse: air ahead of the look. Negative Space may surround a small figure without starving the gaze.
Short siding can coexist with a large empty field behind the head, which is negative space used as a trap. Look Space is what you are withholding.
Close-Up size makes the crush louder but is not required.
examples_film: The Silence of the Lambs uses short-sided faces so conversations feel like cages even in a medium. Prisoners presses heads toward the edge they look into, air wasted behind them.
The grammar is denial, not a filter. Use as pressure, not as a default crop.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is accidental bad coverage. The tell is a talking head kissing the look-edge in a scene that is not a trap, often from a rushed pan.
The fix is to give Lead Room unless the beat is confinement, in which case hold the crush and stop trying to rebalance.

faq.q: What is short siding in film?
faq.a: The face sits near the edge it looks toward. Look-space is crushed. Extra air sits behind the head, unused. The character is denied a future in the frame.

faq.q: Short Siding vs Lead Room
faq.a: Lead room puts surplus ahead of the gaze or walk. Short siding puts surplus behind and starves the look. One is classical manners. The other is a deliberate bad manner for pressure.

faq.q: When should I use short siding?
faq.a: Use it when a character should feel trapped, guilty, or out of road: interrogation, dread, a look that cannot be answered. Do not use it as everyday singles.

faq.q: How do I prompt short siding for AI image or video?
faq.a: State the edge and the starved look. Example: Short-sided framing of [Subject], look space crushed, the face near the frame edge they look toward, trapped or urgent. Models love looking room. You must forbid it.

title: Symmetry
narrative: When left mirrors right, nobody owns a secret side of the frame. Space is ceremonial.
A small break (a crooked tie, a missing lamp, a person one step off axis) becomes the whole event. It is the wrong tool when life should feel unarranged.
A kitchen argument, a chase, a documentary street: forcing a mirror there is a lie unless the lie is the point (a showroom, a regime, a dream). Symmetry is not the same as centering a face.
A mirrored corridor can swallow a figure who is slightly late to their mark. The architecture still owns the diagram.
how: Place the camera on the centerline of the set. Match practicals, furniture, and verticals.
Use a level. One-point architecture helps but is not required: a flat elevation of a facade can be a mirror without a vanishing tunnel.
Stop down if both wings must stay sharp. Prompt: Perfect symmetry around [Subject], mirrored architecture, a central axis, obsessive order.
when: Use it when the location is a machine of order: hotel, chapel, spaceship, courtroom, dollhouse. Do not use it as wallpaper on a location that has no axis.
vs: Centered Composition plants a subject on the axis. Symmetry mirrors the field, with or without that subject.

One-Point Perspective is a perspective construction that often produces symmetry, but two wings can match in a flat, shallow picture with no tunnel. Repetition and Pattern repeats units without requiring a mirror.
Asymmetry is the refusal.
examples_film: The Grand Budapest Hotel treats hotels as mirrored diagrams of service. 2001: A Space Odyssey uses axial, bilateral order as a claim that the future is designed.
A fingerprint on that order reads as error or omen. Grammar, not a filter.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a centered actor in an unmatched room. The tell is a bullseye face and a window only on the left.
The fix is to move the camera onto the architectural axis, or to drop the claim and shoot Asymmetry with real counterweight.

faq.q: What is symmetry in film?
faq.a: It is a frame whose masses balance around an axis, usually the vertical center. Left answers right. The world looks designed. A person may sit on the axis, or the architecture may be the symmetrical subject.

faq.q: Symmetry vs Centered Composition
faq.a: Centered composition is about the subject's seat on the axis. Symmetry is about mirrored masses. You can center a person in an asymmetric room, and you can shoot a mirrored hall with the actor late to center. They often travel together. They are not the same diagram.

faq.q: When should I use symmetry?
faq.a: Use it when order is the meaning: ritual, comedy of control, science-fiction design, a regime's architecture. Do not glue it onto a street that has no axis.

faq.q: How do I prompt symmetry for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for a mirror and an axis. Example: Perfect symmetry around [Subject], mirrored architecture, a central axis, obsessive order. Specify matching practicals and a camera on the centerline. Name one break if the story is the unmatched thing.

title: Tableau
narrative: Hold the arrangement and the audience reads at their own speed: who stands where, who fails to move, who sneaks a gesture. Stillness makes a tiny action loud.
Comedy, ceremony, and dread all use that delay. It is the wrong tool when the scene needs chase geography or a close-up of a lie.
If you cut the tableau to pieces immediately, you shot a master and threw it away. If the arrangement has no readable relationships, you shot decoration.
Tableau is not automatically centered, but it likes a designed field. Dirty edges can still apply if the living picture is glimpsed from a door.
how: Block silhouettes, spacing, and sightlines before adding motion. Rehearse separate timings inside the shared frame.
Use enough depth of field that the intended points stay readable. A locked tripod is the default.
A slow creep is a different sentence. Prompt: Tableau of [Subject], arranged bodies, a living painting, duration instead of coverage.
when: Use it for ritual, comic ensembles, processions, and any beat that should be discovered rather than prescribed by cutting. Do not hold a well-dressed but empty arrangement.
vs: Static Locked-Off is the camera lock. Tableau is the staged picture that uses that lock.
Centered Composition is a common altar for it, not a requirement. Group Shot is a size.
Tableau is duration plus arrangement. Triangular Composition may be the geometry inside the hold.
Long Take may travel. A tableau usually stays and lets time do the move.
examples_film: Barry Lyndon holds painterly courts until a glance is an event. Roy Andersson 's films park ensembles in still rooms so a small failure is comic and awful.
PlayTime distributes gags across broad, held compositions. The Color of Pomegranates arranges people and objects as ritual friezes.
Grammar of duration, not a freeze.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Master Shot you plan to chop, or a pretty still with no relationships. The tell is a posed group that exists to be pretty, then a cut to close-ups that do all the work.
The fix is to give each body a job and to let the hold be the coverage.

faq.q: What is tableau in film?
faq.a: It is a staged picture whose meaning develops inside a relatively fixed frame. Bodies and objects are arranged. Duration does the work that cutting would otherwise do. A living painting, not a freeze frame.

faq.q: Tableau vs Static Locked-Off
faq.a: Static is a camera that does not move. Tableau is an arranged field that uses stillness, usually with a locked camera. You can lock off a messy documentary corner and have static without tableau. You can, rarely, drift across a tableau, but the default is a hold.

faq.q: When should I use tableau?
faq.a: Use it for ritual, ensemble comedy, processions, and any scene the audience should read as a whole. Do not use it as a pretty pause in a chase, and do not cut it to bits immediately.

faq.q: How do I prompt tableau for AI image or video?
faq.a: Describe the arrangement and the hold. Example: Tableau of [Subject], arranged bodies, a living painting, duration instead of coverage. List positions. For video, specify a locked camera and a long hold with one planned gesture.

title: Triangular Composition
narrative: Two people and a desk, a family and a doorway, three men and a gun: the triangle tells you who sits at the top of the diagram. Renaissance blocking taught this before cinema.
The camera inherited the altar. It is the wrong tool for a true two-hander that should be a flat axis, or for a crowd that has no hierarchy.
Forcing a triangle onto two people plus a plant is a fake court. The apex can be low (a child, a corpse, a briefcase) and still run the picture.
Height is not automatically rank. Placement in the triangle is.
how: Block three masses with clear vertices. Check the silhouette on a wide enough lens that all three read (often 27mm to 40mm, or a longer lens at a distance).
Keep depth of field sufficient for the intended points. A Three-Shot is a size.
The triangle is the geometry inside it. Prompt: Triangular arrangement with [Subject] at an apex, three masses locking the frame, Renaissance blocking.
when: Use it when a group has a hierarchy: a don and two captains, a family portrait with a secret, a bargaining table. Do not invent a third mass to complete a shape nobody in the scene would form.
vs: Three-Shot is coverage of three bodies, which may sit in a line. Triangular composition is the pyramid, even if one mass is a doorway or a lamp.
Visual Weight decides which vertex wins the eye. Centered Composition may plant the apex on the axis.
Tableau can freeze the triangle for duration. Symmetry may split a triangle into a formal court.
examples_film: The Godfather uses office blocking as a pyramid of power: who sits, who stands, who waits at the door. Painters' Last Supper language (a central apex, flanking groups) is the ancestor of that court.
Cinema borrowed the altar long before it borrowed the name. Grammar of rank, not a painting to clone.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a flat Three-Shot in a line. The tell is three heads at one height, no pyramid.
The fix is to sit one figure, stand another, and give the third a doorway or a chair so the triangle actually locks.

faq.q: What is triangular composition in film?
faq.a: Subjects or masses form a triangle in the frame. Three points lock the picture. The apex usually holds power, desire, or the thing being judged. The base supports or threatens.

faq.q: Triangular Composition vs Three-Shot
faq.a: A three-shot is a framing size: three people in the picture. They might stand in a row. Triangular composition is geometry. One vertex can even be an object or a doorway. Size is not shape.

faq.q: When should I use triangular composition?
faq.a: Use it when a group has rank or a secret third term: family, court, deal, interrogation. Do not fake a third point with furniture that has no job.

faq.q: How do I prompt triangular composition for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the apex and the other two masses. Example: Triangular arrangement with [Subject] at an apex, three masses locking the frame, Renaissance blocking. State standing versus sitting if height is the hierarchy.

title: Vanishing Point
narrative: There is a long way still to go when the point sits beyond the figure. Space owns the future.
The body is a threshold, not the altar. If the point sits on the face, the architecture aims at them like a weapon or a blessing.
It is the wrong tool in a flat elevation with no receding parallels. A painted backdrop that does not converge cannot offer a vanishing point.
You would be naming a ghost. One-point, two-point, and three-point perspective all have vanishing points.
The compositional choice is where you put them, and whether the subject blocks, occupies, or is ignored by that meeting.
how: Stand where real parallels recede: tracks, a highway, a colonnade. Choose height (eye-level keeps the point near the horizon; a low camera lifts it).
Place the subject on the point, in front of it, or off it. A wider lens makes the suck toward infinity more violent.
Prompt: Deep vanishing point beyond [Subject], rails or road sucking the eye to infinity, the person as a gate.
when: Use it when distance is the meaning: a road, a station, a landing site, a life still unwalked. Do not claim a vanishing point in a flat, shallow room.
vs: One-Point Perspective is the special case of a single, often axial, vanishing point with the camera squared. Vanishing-point composition can be a two-point street corner with the meeting off to the side.
Leading Lines steer the eye but may never meet in frame. Extreme Long Shot often includes a distant point.
The point is a location in the diagram, not a shot size.
examples_film: Paris, Texas aims roads and rails at a horizon that keeps going after the man stops. Close Encounters builds landing-site perspective as a meeting with something that arrives from the point.
Stations, docks, and desert highways are the same grammar: infinity as a character.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a centered figure with no converging lines. The tell is a person in the middle of a flat field and a prompt that only says vanishing.
The fix is to include actual receding parallels, or to switch to Centered Composition and stop claiming perspective.

faq.q: What is a vanishing point in film?
faq.a: It is where parallel lines appear to meet in the picture. Roads, rails, and halls aim there. Compositionally it is a destination: beyond the figure, on the figure, or off to one side.

faq.q: Vanishing Point vs One-Point Perspective
faq.a: One-point perspective uses a single vanishing point and a camera squared to a plane, often on axis. A vanishing point also exists in two-point views of a building corner. One-point is a construction. The vanishing point is the meeting itself.

faq.q: When should I use vanishing point?
faq.a: Use it when distance should act: roads, tracks, naves, anything that still has a long way to go. Skip it in shallow, flat rooms with no receding edges.

faq.q: How do I prompt vanishing point for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the parallels and where they meet. Example: Deep vanishing point beyond [Subject], rails or road sucking the eye to infinity, the person as a gate. If the point should sit on the body, say vanishing point on the chest, architecture aiming at them.

title: Visual Weight
narrative: The diagram is a set of weights, not a ruler. A cigarette in a pool of light can outweigh a sofa.
A face, even tiny, will beat a mountain unless you starve the face of contrast. Who owns space is who wins the glance in the first half second, then the second glance you designed.
It is the wrong tool as a slogan. Saying visual weight without choosing a winner is a wish.
If two masses fight to a draw, the beat is confused unless the fight is the point. Motion and faces cheat.
A still landscape that was balanced becomes a different picture when a figure turns. Recheck weight when action starts.
how: List the masses and their currencies: size, tone, chroma, sharpness, position (center and upper field weigh more), faces, movement. Dim or desaturate the losers, or throw them out of focus.
A hard key on a small object is a common way to mint weight. Prompt: Composition balancing visual weight around [Subject], a bright small thing equal to a large dark mass, scale of attention.
when: Use it whenever more than one mass could steal the shot: a deal on a table, a child in a window, a red coat in a grey street. Do not light every surface equally and hope the script will point.
vs: Asymmetry is often how unequal weights still hold as a picture. Tonal Contrast is specifically tonal punch, lightest versus darkest.
Visual weight includes color, faces, and motion. Figure-Ground is the first-read separation of person from field.
Triangular Composition assigns rank by geometry. Weight can override the apex if you light the wrong vertex.
examples_film: Painterly cinema is a school of weight: a lit hand, a dark coat, a window. Barry Lyndon and other candlelit pictures let a small warm mass equal a room.
Westerns and desert films let a tiny rider equal a butte by placing them on a line and isolating tone. Grammar of attention, not a painting to duplicate.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is even, polite illumination. The tell is every object at the same brightness and sharpness, a catalogue page.
The fix is to pick a winner and tax the rest: darker, softer, smaller, or less chromatic.

faq.q: What is visual weight in film?
faq.a: It is how strongly an element pulls the eye: size, contrast, color, position, focus, faces, motion. A small bright face can outweigh a large dark wall. The first glance should match the story.

faq.q: Visual Weight vs Tonal Contrast
faq.a: Tonal contrast is a graphic fight of light against dark. Visual weight is the broader ledger. Color, faces, and motion count. A mid-grey moving face can outweigh a static white wall.

faq.q: When should I use visual weight?
faq.a: On every frame that contains more than one claim. Consciously, when a small object or distant person must beat a large set. Do not light the room like a showroom unless the showroom is the joke.

faq.q: How do I prompt visual weight for AI image or video?
faq.a: Declare the winner. Example: Composition balancing visual weight around [Subject], a bright small thing equal to a large dark mass, scale of attention. Name both masses. Say the eye lands on the subject first.

title: Void
narrative: Erase the set and the social world goes with it. A woman in a black room, a man in white nowhere, a beam with no walls: there is no furniture to own space, only the figure and the absence.
It is the wrong tool when geography matters. A void cannot show a door, a class, or a weather.
If you still need the kitchen, you wanted negative space or cameo light in a real room. Cameo lighting can create a void by refusing to fill.
The void is the compositional result: no readable world, not merely a moody key.
how: Kill the surround. Black velvet, an unlit stage, fogged white, a clipped sky.
Light only the figure, or let them fall to Silhouette on nothing. Watch for stray stand legs and floor bounce.
A longer lens helps exclude leftover set. Prompt: Void around [Subject], darkness or blank field eating the world, a figure against nothing.
when: Use it for existential isolation, alien rooms, interrogation nowhere, a mind. Do not use it as a cheap way to hide a location you did not dress.
vs: Negative Space keeps a world (sky, wall, sea) as the empty mass. Void removes the world.
Cameo Lighting is the lighting method that often produces a dark void: a pool on a figure, no environment. Clean Frame still allows a tidy place.
Silhouette is outline against a brighter field, which can be a void if that field is featureless. Low-Key Lighting may still show a room in the shadows.
examples_film: Under the Skin uses black, featureless space as a place that is not a place, bodies without social furniture. The Lighthouse isolates men in weather and dark until the world feels eaten, more void than village.
Grammar of deletion, not a crushed exposure accident.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is an underexposed room, or Negative Space with a visible wall. The tell is a baseboard, a plant, or grainy wallpaper in the dark.
The fix is to actually kill the surround (velvet, distance, flags), or to own the wall as designed emptiness.

faq.q: What is void in film?
faq.a: It is a composition that erases the set. The figure stands against darkness, white, or a blank field. There is no readable place. Absence is not a sky or a wall. It is nothing.

faq.q: Void vs Negative Space
faq.a: Negative space is empty area inside a world: desert, ceiling, sea. Void deletes the world. A nun under a pale church wall is negative space. A body in featureless black is a void. Both isolate. Only one still has geography.

faq.q: When should I use void?
faq.a: Use it when place should vanish: alien interior, mind, interrogation nowhere, existential isolation. Do not use it to hide an undressed set that still needs to be a room.

faq.q: How do I prompt void for AI image or video?
faq.a: Forbid the set. Example: Void around [Subject], darkness or blank field eating the world, a figure against nothing. Add no environment, no furniture. Specify black or white. Models love to invent rooms. Ban them.

title: Voyeur
narrative: The audience is trespassing. That is the beat.
A couple through blinds, a conversation across a square, a tent at night: we occupy a hiding place. The subject does not present.
They are caught, or they would be if they turned. It is the wrong tool for granted intimacy.
A close-up the character knows about is not voyeur. An over-the-shoulder in a dialogue scene is coverage, even if a shoulder dirties the edge.
Offscreen sound often rides with this view (a whistle, a courtyard, a tent wall) because the hide limits what we can see. The technique itself is the concealed camera, not the soundtrack.
how: Put a real occluder between lens and subject and stand where a watcher could stand. Keep enough aperture to melt the hide (leaves, fabric, a slit) while holding the distant face.
A longer lens is the usual cheat for distance. Do not center the peephole like a pretty wreath unless the hide is a designed iris.
Prompt: Voyeur frame of [Subject], watching from concealment, dirty edges, a view we should not have.
when: Use it when watching is transgression: affairs, surveillance, a neighbor, a hunter. Do not slap dirty leaves on a scene the character is performing for us.
vs: Dirty Frame is the edge grammar voyeur often uses. Voyeur is the ethical position: concealment.
You can dirty a party from inside the crowd without hiding. Over-the-Shoulder Coverage is dialogue coverage with a known listener in the foreground.
Frame within Frame may be a window we are invited to look through. Windows stacks many lives.
Voyeur picks one hide. Point of View claims we are the character.
Voyeur often claims we are not supposed to be anyone.
examples_film: Rear Window makes looking across a courtyard the plot. The Conversation records and watches until privacy is a myth.

Cache (Hidden) holds distant, unauthorized views until the camera itself is an aggressor. M and The Blair Witch Project let presence arrive from beyond the visible, often as sound around a limited hide.
Grammar of trespass, not a leaf kit.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a pretty Dirty Frame the subject could see, or an Over-the-Shoulder Coverage from a scene partner. The tell is eye contact with lens, or a hide that is only a vignette.
The fix is a real occluder, a plausible hiding place, and a subject who does not present.

faq.q: What is voyeur in film?
faq.a: The camera watches from concealment. The audience is trespassing. Dirty edges, distance, and a peephole often result. The subject does not offer the view. We take it.

faq.q: Voyeur vs Dirty Frame
faq.a: A dirty frame occupies the edges with matter. Voyeur is why we are standing there: we are hidden. A crowded street can be dirty without being voyeur. A clean, distant locked-off shot of an apartment can be voyeur without much edge chew, as in an unauthorized surveillance hold.

faq.q: When should I use voyeur?
faq.a: Use it when looking is a transgression: neighbor, spy, hunter, affair. Do not use it as default decoration on a scene performed for the camera.

faq.q: How do I prompt voyeur for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the concealment and the unaware subject. Example: Voyeur frame of [Subject], watching from concealment, dirty edges, a view we should not have. Specify blinds, foliage, a grate, a long lens. Forbid eye contact with camera.

title: Windows
narrative: A facade at night is a contact sheet of other people's rooms. A courtyard is a theater of windows.
Who owns space changes per rectangle: a cook, a sleeper, a fighter, an empty kitchen. The building is a montage that does not cut.
It is the wrong tool when you only need one inner frame around one encounter. That is a single frame-within-frame.
If the other panes do no work, you photographed a house. Windows can be looked through from inside (rain on glass, a face and a street) or looked at from outside ( Rear Window grammar).
Decide which side of the glass we occupy, and whether reflections will stack a second world.
how: Find a true grid: a courtyard, a block of apartments, an office elevation. Use a longer lens to flatten panes into a sheet of rectangles, or a wider lens if we are inside one room looking at many across a court.

Expose so more than one interior reads, or so most go dark except the one that matters. Prompt: Windows as the true subject around [Subject], stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames.
when: Use it when many lives share a building, or when a single life is one pane among others. Do not use it as a pretty rain window on a portrait that never acknowledges other rooms.
vs: Frame within Frame is usually one inner rectangle. Windows multiplies them.
Screen in Screen nests electronic pictures. These are architectural pictures.
Voyeur may watch one pane from concealment. Windows can also be a public elevation, a city showing itself.
Repetition and Pattern counts the grid. Here the content of each cell matters.
Reflections may write the street onto the same glass.
examples_film: Rear Window turns a courtyard of windows into a set of simultaneous shorts. The Hours uses windows as thresholds between interior lives and the weather of a city.
A building becomes an editing machine you can hold. Grammar of panes, not a single pretty rain glass.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a single rain-streaked portrait, or a Frame within Frame doorway. The tell is one face and one glass with no other cells.
The fix is to show a grid of apertures and to give at least one other pane a life, even if it is only a lamp and an empty chair.

faq.q: What is windows in film?
faq.a: Panes become the subject: stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames. The composition is a grid of possible shots. One person may occupy one cell. The other cells still work.

faq.q: Windows vs Frame within Frame
faq.a: Frame within a frame is typically one inner border around the action, a door or arch. Windows multiplies apertures until the building is a sheet of pictures. A single window around a couple is doorway grammar. A courtyard of ten lit rooms is windows.

faq.q: When should I use windows?
faq.a: Use it when many lives share glass: apartments, offices, a courtyard at night, a city block. Skip it when you only need one threshold around one encounter.

faq.q: How do I prompt windows for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for stacked panes and multiple lives. Example: Windows as the true subject around [Subject], stacked apertures, lives in rectangles, a building of frames. Specify a facade or courtyard and more than one lit interior. Place the subject in one cell.

title: Axial Cut
narrative: A farmhouse kitchen, then the same kitchen larger, then an eye socket you were not ready to occupy. Recognition arrives as a series of shocks, not as a walk.
Change shot size without changing angle. Use it for stepwise emphasis: a date in a book, a wound, a face that must suddenly fill the world.
It is the wrong tool when you want a continuous approach. A Crash Zoom In is an optical move in time.
A dolly-in is a walk. An axial cut is an edit.
If the angle changes more than a few degrees, you have ordinary coverage, not an axial cut. If time is what you skipped inside one size, you have a Jump Cut .
how: Capture or generate matched wide, medium, and close compositions on the same axis. Preserve pose, eyeline, and background alignment enough that the jump is only scale.
Choose deliberate steps (for example 50mm at 3 meters, then 50mm at 1 meter, or a punch-in crop that matches a true closer camera). Do not animate a zoom between the frames if the point is the snap.
Prompt: axial cut jumping toward or away from [Subject] along the lens axis, punch-in without a zoom.
when: Use it when a detail must land as a blow: the date stamp, the empty eye, the gun on the table. Do not use it as a substitute for a motivated push-in during a long take.
If the camera should walk, walk.
vs: A Crash Zoom In is a continuous, fast focal-length change. An axial cut is a splice.
A Jump Cut skips time in a similar size; axial cut skips distance on one axis. Match on Action needs a bridging gesture; axial cut can hit a still figure.
A push-in has parallax; a punch-in crop of one take has none, and is a cheaper cousin of a true closer camera on the same axis.
examples_film: The Birds sends Lydia through successive closer views of the dead farmer, the axis held, the scale jumping. The Shining uses hard axial emphasis on rooms and faces so space feels like a trap.
Goodfellas punches in for recognition rather than a polite zoom. Use the snap, not a copied kitchen.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Crash Zoom In or a digital crop sold as a camera move. The tell: the lens breathes, or the angle walks off axis, or the subject morphs larger.
The fix: two (or three) still-matched compositions, same axis, hard cuts, pose locked.

faq.q: What is Axial Cut in film?
faq.a: An axial cut jumps closer or farther along the same camera axis. Both sides of the join share an angle; only shot size changes, as a snap rather than a move.

faq.q: Axial Cut vs Crash Zoom In
faq.a: A crash zoom is a continuous optical move. An axial cut is an edit between matched distances on one axis. One is a whoosh; the other is a punch.

faq.q: When should I use Axial Cut?
faq.a: Use it to change shot size without changing angle, when recognition should shock. Do not use it when you want the camera to walk or the lens to zoom in time.

faq.q: How do I prompt Axial Cut for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for matched wide and close frames on the same axis, then a hard cut. Example: Axial cut jumping toward [Subject] along the lens axis, punch-in without a zoom. No zoom animation.

title: Crash Cut
narrative: A trunk, a man, a knife already in play, then the story will explain how we got here. Or a cymbal, a face, a rehearsal that never had a polite establishing wide.
The next image must hurt, and it must hurt immediately. Use it as percussion, as in medias res, as a refusal of the soft open.
It is the wrong tool when you have just built a hush that should be betrayed: that betrayal is a Smash Cut . It is the wrong tool when you only skip time in one seat: that is a Jump Cut .
A few frames of interrupt are a Flash Cut , not a committed new scene. Do not open on a sensation the rest of the story cannot causally earn.
how: Cut A to B with maximum difference in scale, brightness, or violence of content, and with no mix. Often B is already mid-action (a trunk, a gun, a kit).

Mark any later temporal reset clearly (a title, a younger haircut) so the crash is a structure, not an accident. Prompt: crash cut on [Subject], two images colliding with no polite blend, a hard join that should sting.
when: Use it to open on the consequence, to hit a downbeat, to refuse an establishing courtesy. Do not use it between two similar wides.
If A was a long prayer, consider smash. If B lasts three frames, consider flash.
vs: A Smash Cut breaks an earned state (quiet, closure, prayer). A crash cut is the collision as a blow, often before a state was offered.
A Jump Cut stays similar. A Flash Cut is too short to become the new scene.
Quick Cuts are a run of short shots; a crash is one brutal splice.
examples_film: Goodfellas opens in the trunk, then later supplies the life that led there. Fight Club starts inside a crisis and then rewinds the path.
Whiplash and Requiem for a Dream use hard joins as rhythmic blows. Use the sting and the delayed explanation, not a copied trunk.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Smash Cut (after a hush) or Flash Cut (a few frames). The tell: a long quiet setup before the hit (that is smash), or B vanishing before it can be a scene (that is flash).
The fix: collide two committed images, start inside the event if that is the structure, cut hard.

faq.q: What is Crash Cut in film?
faq.a: A crash cut is a hard join where two images collide with no blend. Both sides are committed shots; the splice stings, often by starting inside an event or hitting like a drum.

faq.q: Crash Cut vs Smash Cut
faq.a: A smash cut betrays an earned quiet or closure. A crash cut is the collision itself, frequently from the first frame of a scene or as in medias res. Smash breaks a state; crash refuses to offer one.

faq.q: When should I use Crash Cut?
faq.a: Use it when the next image must hurt immediately, or when the story should start inside the consequence. Do not use it as a skip inside one similar frame.

faq.q: How do I prompt Crash Cut for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name two colliding images and forbid a blend. Example: Crash cut on [Subject], two images colliding with no polite blend, a hard join that should sting. Let B be mid-action if the structure needs it.

title: Cross-Cutting
narrative: A baptism in one room. Killings in others.
The film does not wait for one to finish. It braids them so ritual and murder share a tense.

Or: a team at a door, a listener at another door, and the cut teaches you they are about to meet until a reverse proves they are not. Use it when simultaneity, comparison, or false geography is the engine.
It is the wrong tool when you need one compressed idea from unlike images: that is Montage . It is also the wrong tool when two rooms must be visible at once: that is Split Screen .
Fair misdirection relies on inference. Do not show matching house numbers and then pretend the doors were different.
how: Shoot each line so it can be interrupted: clear geography, readable time of day or clock, compatible but not identical details if you plan a wrong-door surprise. Alternate with tightening duration if you want the clocks to race.
Sound can bleed across (a bell, a vow) to bind the lines. Prompt: cross-cutting between [Subject] and a simultaneous other line, suspense by alternation, two clocks racing.
when: Use it for a raid versus a doorbell, a ritual versus a crime, dream levels that must tick together. Do not use it to dump unused coverage of one scene.
If there is no second clock, you are just cutting.
vs: Montage collides images to make an argument or to compress months; cross-cutting keeps parallel actions alive. A Smash Cut is one contrast join, not a braid.
Split Screen shows both lines at once instead of alternating. An L-cut lets sound from one line sit on the picture of the other without changing the picture's location.
examples_film: The Godfather baptizes Michael while the rival killings land in other rooms. The Silence of the Lambs intercuts an FBI raid with a doorbell, then reveals the geography was wrong.
Inception alternates dream levels so one clock pressures another. Use the braid, not the blocking.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Montage (idea by collision) or Split Screen (both at once). The tell: the second line has no clock, or both lines are clearly the same hallway.
The fix: two geographies, implied simultaneity, a reveal if you are lying about the door.

faq.q: What is Cross-Cutting in film?
faq.a: Cross-cutting alternates locations or action lines, usually to imply they are simultaneous. Each side of the join is its own strand; the cut says meanwhile.

faq.q: Cross-Cutting vs Montage
faq.a: Montage juxtaposes shots to compress time or produce an idea. Cross-cutting keeps two (or more) ongoing actions in play and braids them. One argues; the other races clocks.

faq.q: When should I use Cross-Cutting?
faq.a: Use it when two lines must tick together: raid and doorbell, vow and murder, two escapes. Do not use it as a pile of unused singles from one room.

faq.q: How do I prompt Cross-Cutting for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name both spaces and the race. Example: Cross-cutting between [Subject] and a simultaneous other line, two clocks racing. Keep the geographies distinct and the assumption of contact clear.

title: Dissolve
narrative: A face thins. A landscape thickens through it.
Time has passed, or memory has, and the cut did not want to be a door slam. Dissolves are for passage, recollection, or the gentle death of a scene.
It is the wrong tool when the next image should hurt, or when the correspondence should snap. Hurt is a Smash Cut .
Snap-rhyme is a Match Cut or Graphic Match . If you hold the overlap as a meaning in itself, you are in Double Exposure territory, not a transition.
A dissolve does not automatically mean years have passed. Duration, sound, and context do that work.
A two-frame dissolve is just a soft cut.
how: Mix A and B over time: typically a dozen frames to a few seconds. Keep a shared compositional hook if you want the overlap to read (a fan through a rotor, a face through a ceiling).
Decide whether sound dissolves with picture or bridges first. This is an optical or digital mix, not a camera move.
Prompt: dissolve from [Subject] into another time or place, overlapping ghosts, longer than a cut admits.
when: Use it for memory, montage-like passage, or a scene that should die instead of stop. Do not use it to hide a bad match on action.
If the two sides should collide, cut hard.
vs: A Fade In / Fade Out goes to a uniform field (black or color) so there is a moment with no scene. A dissolve never empties the frame; B is already there.
Double Exposure holds two images as a stacked meaning, not as a handoff. Morph warps contours; dissolve only changes opacity.
Wipe uses a traveling boundary instead of a mix.
examples_film: Citizen Kane uses dissolves as time's grammar through a life. The Godfather lets faces and rooms bleed across turns of power.
Apocalypse Now layers hotel fan, jungle, and helicopter so picture and sound dissolve together. The 39 Steps bridges a scream into a train whistle, a sonic cousin of the mix.
Grammar of overlap, not a look to steal.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Fade In / Fade Out (empty field in the middle) or a morph . The tell: the frame goes to black, or A warps into B.
The fix: keep both pictures intact, change only opacity, let the midpoint show two readable images.

faq.q: What is Dissolve in film?
faq.a: A dissolve overlaps the outgoing shot with the incoming shot so both are visible for a duration. One side fades in presence while the other takes over; there is no empty field in between.

faq.q: Dissolve vs Fade In / Fade Out
faq.a: A fade goes to or from a uniform black or color field, a pause with no scene. A dissolve hands one picture to another through a mix. Fade punctuates; dissolve bleeds.

faq.q: When should I use Dissolve?
faq.a: Use it for memory, elapsed time, or a scene that should die softly. Do not use it when the next image should smash or when a hard graphic rhyme is the point.

faq.q: How do I prompt Dissolve for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name both shots and the overlap. Example: Dissolve from [Subject] into another time or place, overlapping ghosts. Specify a mix, not a morph, and how long the ghosts share the frame.

title: Fade In / Fade Out
narrative: The room goes. Red remains, or black does, long enough to feel like a closed book.
Then another room is born from the same field. A fade is punctuation, not a mix of two stories.

Use it when a scene is a chapter, when consciousness drops, or when you want a pause the audience can rest in. It is the wrong tool for a gentle bleed between two images that should both stay present: that is a Dissolve .
It is also the wrong tool if you only want to point at a face inside a shrinking circle: that is an Iris . A fade does not automatically mean a long period has passed.
Sound that continues over black can mean a second of unconsciousness. Sound that dies with the picture can mean an ending.
how: Reduce the picture to a field (or raise a picture out of one). Choose black for neutral chaptering, or a color (deep red, white) when the field itself should feel like a mood.
Coordinate whether sound survives the empty picture. Do not fill the room with fog or smoke to fake a fade; the image must leave, not get weather.
Prompt: fade to or from black around [Subject], chapter punctuation, sleep, death, or the start of a world.
when: Use it to open a film, close an act, or mark a blackout of awareness. Do not use it between every scene in a contemporary dialogue piece unless you want a period cadence.
If two pictures should overlap, dissolve.
vs: A Dissolve overlaps two scenes; a fade empties the frame first. An Iris is a moving mask that points at a detail while the rest goes black, not a full-field fade.
A Wipe keeps both pictures alive, divided by a traveling edge. Vignette is optical falloff on a living image, not a transition.
examples_film: Cries and Whispers uses red fields as emotional punctuation between rooms and crises. 1917 uses a blackout to separate lapse and return of consciousness.
Classical studio films chapter with fades to black as a default. Borrow the pause, not a tint as a trademark.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Dissolve (two pictures mixed) or fog as a fake fade. ' The fix: go to a uniform field, hold it, then let the next scene emerge.
No overlap, no weather.

faq.q: What is Fade In / Fade Out in film?
faq.a: A fade takes the image to or from a uniform black or color field. One side of the join is a scene; the other is absence, not another picture mixed on top.

faq.q: Fade In / Fade Out vs Dissolve
faq.a: A dissolve overlaps two shots so both are visible at once. A fade inserts a field of black or color between worlds. Dissolve bleeds; fade punctuates.

faq.q: When should I use Fade In / Fade Out?
faq.a: Use it for chapter breaks, openings, endings, sleep, or a loss of consciousness. Do not use it as a blend between two images that should share the frame.

faq.q: How do I prompt Fade In / Fade Out for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the subject and the field. Example: Fade to or from black around [Subject], chapter punctuation. Say whether sound continues over the empty field, and do not fake it with smoke.

title: Flash Cut
narrative: A face in a room. Three frames of a well, a tape, a child.
The room again. You cannot inventory what you saw, but it has already happened to you.
A thought that lasts three frames. Use it for intrusion: prophecy wearing the clothes of memory, a trauma tic, a subliminal threat.
It is the wrong tool when the other image should become the scene. That committed landing is a Crash Cut or Smash Cut .
A white frame that is only exposure is a Light Flash , not another picture. Keep the insert temporally honest enough that a later anchor can fix it.
Mystery is not the same as no clue.
how: Hold the present shot. Insert 1 to 8 frames of a different image (often high contrast, closer, or from another time).
Return to the present, or chain flashes. Do not dissolve; the brevity is the grammar.
Picture may be silent or carry a tick of sound. Prompt: flash cut through [Subject], a few frames of another image interrupting, lightning in the edit.
when: Use it when a mind is leaking another time, or when a threat should be unreadable but present. Do not use it as decoration on a trailer.
If the audience must read the insert, give it a shot, not a flash.
vs: A Crash Cut stays with the new image. A Light Flash is a burst of light, not a second diegesis.
A Jump Cut skips time in a similar frame without inserting a foreign picture. Smash Cut commits to contrast as the new present.
Flash cut is an interrupt.
examples_film: The Ring uses stolen frames as contamination. Natural Born Killers sprays interruptive images as a nervous system.
Arrival presents images that first read as memory and are later re-placed in time. Use the brevity and the later anchor, not a copied well.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Light Flash (no second image) or Crash Cut (the insert stays). The tell: a white blink, or a new scene that never returns to the present.
The fix: a countable handful of frames of a different picture, then the original scene, hard cuts.

faq.q: What is Flash Cut in film?
faq.a: A flash cut inserts a few frames of another image into an ongoing shot. One side is the present; the other is a blink of a different picture, too short to become the scene.

faq.q: Flash Cut vs Crash Cut
faq.a: A crash cut lands in a new committed image. A flash cut interrupts and (usually) returns. Duration is the difference: a scene versus a handful of frames.

faq.q: When should I use Flash Cut?
faq.a: Use it for a thought, a leak of another time, or a threat too brief to inventory. Do not use it when the other image needs to be read as the new present.

faq.q: How do I prompt Flash Cut for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the present shot, the insert, and the frame count. Example: Flash cut through [Subject], a few frames of another image interrupting. Hard cuts, no dissolve, then return.

title: Fragments
narrative: You never get the master. You get a sleeve, a missed catch, a face, ceramic already on the floor, and one offscreen crash.
Do not give the whole. The viewer assembles the blow.
Use it to make an impact intense while withholding explicit depiction, or to show a night that will not assemble. It is the wrong tool when the audience must see a legal, continuous action.
It is also not just speed: Quick Cuts can show complete blows rapidly. Fragments hide the complete blow.
Fast shards alone do not guarantee clarity. Direction, causal order, and sound have to let the viewer reconstruct the event.
how: Break the event into distinct visual elements that can be shot safely: the approaching object, a body part, a reaction, the aftermath. Preserve screen direction and order.
Bind with timing and sound; do not require the dangerous contact on camera. Prompt: fragments of [Subject], shattered coverage, pieces of a moment, the scene as shards.
Name what is missing.
when: Use it for a shower, a staircase massacre built from details, a panic, a memory. Do not use it for a demonstration that must be readable as one take.
If the pieces cannot be ordered into a cause, you have a Collage , not an event.
vs: Quick Cuts are a rate pattern and may show complete actions. Montage collides complete images for an idea or a month.
Collage is a paper or composite of pieces as a surface. Jump Cut holes one setup.
Fragments are incomplete views of one action whose whole is inferred.
examples_film: Psycho constructs the shower from brief fragments, reactions, and sound rather than one continuous explicit view. Battleship Potemkin builds the Odessa Steps from details and reactions.
Requiem for a Dream and Memento use shards as a nervous or backward structure. Use inference, not a copied stab.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Quick Cuts of the same complete wide, or a Collage texture. The tell: a master already shows the whole, or the pieces have no direction.
The fix: withhold the complete contact, keep a causal line, let sound and order finish the blow in the viewer's head.

faq.q: What is Fragments in film?
faq.a: Fragmented editing constructs an event from partial views. Each side of a join is a shard; the audience infers an action more complete than any single shot.

faq.q: Fragments vs Quick Cuts
faq.a: Quick cuts are short complete views in a rhythm. Fragments are incomplete views of one event. Speed is not the definition; withholding the whole is.

faq.q: When should I use Fragments?
faq.a: Use it when the blow should be inferred: violence, panic, a night that will not assemble. Do not use it when a continuous demonstration is required.

faq.q: How do I prompt Fragments for AI image or video?
faq.a: List the shards and what is missing. Example: Fragments of [Subject], shattered coverage, pieces of a moment. Keep causal order and a binding sound; forbid a complete master of the contact.

title: Graphic Match
narrative: You leave a drain, circular, centered. You arrive on an eye, circular, centered.
Nothing has been explained, but the cut has already made a bridge. The viewer feels the leap before anyone names it.
Use it when form should carry you across time or place. It is the wrong tool when the two frames do not share a contour you can point at.
Matching wardrobe or actor identity is not a graphic match. A graphic match is not a morph.
Similarity across a hard cut is enough. If the image melts, you have left editing and entered morph .
how: Design the outgoing and incoming frames together. Match the important contour and screen position rather than every part of the image: circle size, horizon height, the diagonal of a body.
Use a hard cut when the instant connection is the point. A short Dissolve can soften the rhyme, but it also hides how precise the match was.
Prompt the silhouette or the echoed shape on both sides, same placement, no morph.
when: Use it when a silhouette, a circle, or a line should survive a jump in time: a watch face to a dome, a scream-mouth to a tunnel. Do not use it as wallpaper between unrelated wides.
If the contour does not match, the cut is just a cut.
vs: A Match Cut may include a graphic rhyme, but it also claims an idea. Graphic match can be purely formal.
Match on Action continues one gesture in one scene. Dissolve overlaps two images in time instead of snapping form to form.
Morph interpolates; graphic match does not.
examples_film: 2001: A Space Odyssey throws a bone and finds a craft of similar attitude and screen path. Psycho leaves the shower drain and arrives on Marion's eye, two circles in one place.
Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown uses compositional rhymes to connect successive images. Borrow the geometry, not the posters.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is morph or a lazy Match Cut that only repeats the actor. The tell: the model blends A into B, or the second frame does not occupy the same contour.
The fix: lock one shape and one placement, keep two different objects, cut hard.

faq.q: What is Graphic Match in film?
faq.a: A graphic match is a cut that connects images with similar shape, line, color, placement, or movement pattern. The two sides of the join can be different places and times; the shared form is the bridge.

faq.q: Graphic Match vs Match Cut
faq.a: Graphic match is a form rhyme. Match cut is a correspondence that can include form but also idea, space, or sound. Many famous joins are both; the graphic match name is about the contour, not the thesis.

faq.q: When should I use Graphic Match?
faq.a: Use it when form should carry the viewer across a leap in time or place. Do not use it when the two frames share no readable contour.

faq.q: How do I prompt Graphic Match for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the silhouette or shape on both sides and put it in the same screen place. Example: Graphic match on the silhouette of [Subject], circle to circle. Demand a hard cut and two distinct objects.

title: Invisible Cut
narrative: A coat fills the lens. When it leaves, the room is later, or the body is gone, or the street has changed.
You needed a cut the audience must not feel. Stop-trick cinema did this with a locked camera and a substitution.
Contemporary oners do it with whips, walls, and stitches. Use it to simulate a long take, to vanish a person, or to change time inside an apparently continuous walk.
It is the wrong tool when the cut should be a sentence: a Match Cut , a Smash Cut , a Wipe . If you want the join seen, do not hide it.
The trick depends on spatial continuity around the substitution. A wandering unmatched camera exposes an unintended jump.
how: Plan a hiding place: a passing body, a dark wall, a whip-pan blur, a matched doorway, a digital stitch on a texture. Lock exposure and lighting across plates if you are substituting.
For a stop trick, lock the camera, hold actors, change the object, splice on the occlusion. For an oner illusion, match motion blur and grain at the whip.
Prompt: invisible cut hidden in [Subject]'s whip, a dark wall, or a passing body, the oner illusion.
when: Use it to extend a take through a theatre, a trench, a street, or to make a woman vanish from a chair. Do not use it to avoid writing a scene change.
If the geography actually transforms as you watch, that may be a Set Transition instead of a hidden splice.
vs: A Oner is the long take you are faking or actually shooting. A Whip Pan can be the bandage over the splice.
Match on Action hides a cut in a readable gesture but still changes the view on purpose. Set Transition lets the location rewrite itself.
Morph is a visible interpolation, the opposite of invisible.
examples_film: The Vanishing Lady substitutes a seated woman between frames. A Trip to the Moon pops Selenites out of existence.
Rope hides joins in dark foregrounds. 1917 and Birdman stitch walks so trenches and theatres feel continuous.
Spectre 's opening presents multiple spaces as one shot. Grammar of concealment, not a take to clone.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a visible Whip Pan that never hides a join, or a morph . The tell: a pop in grain, a jump in crowd, a morphing wall.
The fix: a true occluder or blur that fills the frame, matched lighting, a hard splice inside that fill, continuous motion on both sides.

faq.q: What is Invisible Cut in film?
faq.a: An invisible cut hides the edit in motion, darkness, occlusion, blur, matching geometry, or stitching. Both sides of the join are meant to play as one continuous shot.

faq.q: Invisible Cut vs Oner
faq.a: A oner is a long take. An invisible cut is how you fake or extend one: the splice sits inside a whip, a wall, or a passing body. One is the apparent shot; the other is the seam.

faq.q: When should I use Invisible Cut?
faq.a: Use it when the audience must not feel the edit: a vanishing act, a stitched walk, a time jump inside a continuous-looking path. Do not use it when the join should speak.

faq.q: How do I prompt Invisible Cut for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the hiding place and both plates. Example: Invisible cut hidden in [Subject]'s whip, a dark wall, or a passing body. Demand matched lighting and no morph.

title: Iris
narrative: The hall is there. The circle tightens on a satisfied face, then opens a little to include the yawning cat on the piano, then shuts.
Silent comedy pointed with the mask itself. The iris is a wink and a chapter ending at once.
Use it to isolate a comic detail, imitate a viewing device, or close in an openly theatrical way. It is the wrong tool if you only want the image to die evenly: that is a Fade In / Fade Out .
It is also not a zoom into a dark tunnel. The camera can sit still while the mask moves.
An iris is a mask over the image, not a Vignette . Vignette is optical falloff on a living frame.
Iris is a boundary that travels until the picture is gone or born.
how: Build the mask in post (or in-camera with an iris gimmick). Control center, shape, and timing.
Decide whether the circle follows a subject or stays fixed while action continues underneath. Iris-in opens from black; iris-out closes to black (or to a tiny remaining image).
Prompt: iris in or out on [Subject], a circular mask closing on a face or detail, silent-era pointing, or a wink.
when: Use it to point at a ring, a glance, a gag, or to end a scene as theatre. Do not use it as a substitute for a push-in.
If the camera must physically approach, move the camera. If the world should fade as a whole, fade.
vs: A Fade In / Fade Out empties the whole field evenly. A Wipe uses a traveling straight or clock edge, not a hole from a center.
Vignette darkens corners without being a transition. A zoom changes focal length; the iris does not.
Match Cut joins two full frames; iris withholds the frame on purpose.
examples_film: Neighbors uses a circular reveal to change the apparent scale and circumstances of a wedding. The Artist borrows silent-era punctuation, including iris-like framing, as a period grammar.
Silent comedy at large treated the iris as a pointing finger. Use the mask logic, not a pastiche overlay on every close-up.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a zoom, a Fade In / Fade Out , or a heavy Vignette . The tell: the camera pushes in, or the whole frame dims evenly, or corners are just dark.
The fix: keep the camera still, animate a circular mask with a chosen center, let the unmasked picture stay at full exposure.

faq.q: What is Iris in film?
faq.a: An iris is a moving circular or shaped mask that reveals or conceals part of the image. One side of the join is the open picture; the other is a pointing hole, often closing to black.

faq.q: Iris vs Fade In / Fade Out
faq.a: A fade takes the entire image to a uniform field. An iris keeps a chosen center visible while the mask closes or opens. Fade is a chapter; iris is a finger.

faq.q: When should I use Iris?
faq.a: Use it to point at a detail, end a gag, or quote silent-era punctuation. Do not use it when you mean a zoom or an even fade to black.

faq.q: How do I prompt Iris for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the subject and the mask. Example: Iris in or out on [Subject], a circular mask closing on a face or detail. Specify center and direction (in or out), and say it is a mask, not a zoom.

title: Jump Cut
narrative: The car is the same. The road is the same.
The speaker has jumped three sentences and a mile. You are not soothed.
The film has shown the skip. Use it for impatience, instability, comic abbreviation, or an openly constructed voice.
It is the wrong tool when you want invisible continuity. If the two frames are very different in size or angle, the skip hides and you have ordinary coverage, not a jump cut.
A jump cut is not simply any fast cut. The visible break within a similar setup is the whole point.
how: Remove intervals from one setup, or join closely related views of the same subject. Keep enough of the composition (lens, angle, body size) that the jump is obvious.
Decide whether sound smooths the skip (a continuous line) or emphasizes it (hard in and out). Prompt: time skipped inside a similar framing, same seat, missing frames, no morph.
when: Use it in a wait, a rambling talk, a comedown, a drive that should feel too long and too short at once. Do not use it as a substitute for coverage you did not shoot.
If the audience should not notice the edit, use Match on Action or an Invisible Cut .
vs: A Smash Cut slams into a violently different image. A jump cut stays inside a similar frame and skips time.
Montage juxtaposes many shots to compress or argue; jump cut is usually one setup with holes. An Axial Cut jumps distance on the same axis as emphasis, not as missing time.
Quick Cuts are short shots from changing setups, a rhythm, not a skip inside one frame.
examples_film: Breathless lets car rides and talks skip forward inside similar framings, which is the modern template. Dancer in the Dark uses discontinuous cutting to disrupt smooth observation.
Requiem for a Dream turns repeated rituals into jumps that feel like appetite. Grammar, not a look to clone.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Quick Cuts or random coverage labeled as a jump. The tell: every shot is a new angle, so nothing jumps.
Or the model morphs the sitter from pose to pose. The fix: keep the framing nearly constant, remove time, let the discontinuity show.

faq.q: What is Jump Cut in film?
faq.a: A jump cut removes time while leaving enough similarity of framing or subject that the break is obvious. Both sides of the join look like the same shot with a hole in it.

faq.q: Jump Cut vs Smash Cut
faq.a: A jump cut skips time inside a similar setup. A smash cut leaves that setup for a violently different image, sound, or scale. One shows a hole; the other shows a collision.

faq.q: When should I use Jump Cut?
faq.a: Use it when the skip itself is the meaning: wait, nerves, comic speed, a narrator who will not pretend the cut is invisible. Do not use it to hide missing coverage.

faq.q: How do I prompt Jump Cut for AI image or video?
faq.a: Keep one framing and skip time inside it. Example: Jump cut on [Subject], time skipped inside a similar framing. Name what changes between jumps and forbid morphing.

title: J-Cut / L-Cut (Visual Setup)
narrative: We hear the next room before we see it (J-cut): the picture stays on the walker, the voice has already arrived. Or we see the listener while the speaker's words continue (L-cut): the face is the bridge.
Sound will lead or lag. The face is the bridge.

Use it when picture and track should not cut on the same frame, so thought can cross a doorway. It is the wrong tool when you need both rooms visible at once ( Split Screen ) or when you only need a mute reaction insert with no overlapping track.
Randomly mismatched music is not automatically meaningful counterpoint. Define what the lag reveals: dread, irony, a voice that will not let the face go.
how: On the timeline, a J-cut lets incoming audio start under the outgoing picture. An L-cut lets outgoing audio continue under the incoming picture.
The visual setup is a shot that can bear that overlap: a Reaction Shot , a walk toward a door, an empty office. Keep the sound's source clear enough that the overlap is information, not muddle.
Prompt: a frame of [Subject] designed as the picture half of an L-cut or J-cut, reaction holding while another space is already speaking.
when: Use it to enter a conversation before the room, to stay on a listener after a confession, to let a song continue over a packing scene it does not belong to. Do not use it as default dialogue cutting if both faces should share the same on-camera words.
If you need meanwhile geography, Cross-Cutting .
vs: A Reaction Shot is the picture; J-cut and L-cut are how that picture meets sound. Cross-Cutting alternates whole lines.
A smash in sound on a picture cut is closer to Smash Cut . Counterpoint (cheerful music on a cruel image) can ride an L-cut, but the technique here is the staggered splice, not the playlist.
examples_film: The Social Network and Heat keep speech living over listeners' faces so thought continues across the join. The Conversation makes incoming sound a threat before the picture explains it.
Yi Yi lets piano arrive before its source is located. A Clockwork Orange and Reservoir Dogs place cheerful tracks against behavior the picture will not bless.
Use the stagger, not the needle-drop.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a mute Reaction Shot with picture and sound cutting together, or a Cross-Cutting that never overlaps track. The tell: lips in the new room are already talking in sync at the picture cut, with no pre-lap.
The fix: hold the first picture while the second track starts, or hold the first track after the picture has moved.

faq.q: What is J-Cut / L-Cut (Visual Setup) in film?
faq.a: A J-cut starts the next shot's sound before its picture; an L-cut keeps the last shot's sound after the picture has changed. The visual setup is a frame that can hold while the other space speaks.

faq.q: J-Cut / L-Cut vs Reaction Shot
faq.a: A reaction shot is a picture of listening. J-cut and L-cut are how that picture is joined to another space's sound. You can have a reaction with a straight cut; the J/L is the stagger.

faq.q: When should I use J-Cut / L-Cut (Visual Setup)?
faq.a: Use it when sound should lead a scene in, or linger after we have left. Do not use it if picture and track must hit together as a smash.

faq.q: How do I prompt J-Cut / L-Cut (Visual Setup) for AI image or video?
faq.a: Describe a face or room that can hold offscreen voice. Example: A frame of [Subject] as the picture half of an L-cut or J-cut, reaction holding while another space is already speaking. For video, say which track pre-laps.

title: Match on Action
narrative: A hand reaches for a handle in a wide. In the close shot the same hand, same speed, same sleeve, finishes the turn.
The viewer follows the reach instead of inspecting the splice. That is the job: hide the cut in a movement.
It is the wrong tool when the action is not continuous, or when you want the skip to be seen. Skipping time inside a similar frame is a Jump Cut .

Jumping closer on the same axis without a bridging gesture is an Axial Cut . If hands swap, travel reverses, or too much of the motion is repeated on both sides, the glue fails and the cut becomes visible for the wrong reason.
how: Repeat the action with matching speed, hand, object position, and body orientation. Cut at a readable phase of motion, usually the acceleration or the midpoint, not after the gesture has already landed.
Check screen direction and sound continuity across the join. The two sides are the same event, different views.
Prompt: the motion started in one shot and finished in the next, same hand, same object, two framings.
when: Use it to change shot size or angle on a door, a punch, a sit-down, a pour. Do not use it to leap to another day or another room.
If the world changes while the vector continues, that is Match Motion , not match on action.
vs: A Match Cut rhymes two different images. Match on action is one action, two views.
An Axial Cut jumps distance on the same axis and does not need a bridging gesture. Match Motion can carry a body into another location or reality if direction and speed match.
Invisible Cut hides the splice in occlusion or blur, not in a readable gesture.
examples_film: Buster Keaton's Neighbors connects courtyard movement across changing views so the body remains the through-line. The Matrix links action across changing shot sizes and viewpoints while the gesture continues.
Classical continuity comedy and action both depend on this glue. Use the principle, not a copied punch.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Jump Cut (time skipped, similar frame) or an Axial Cut (scale jump, no bridging move). The tell: the close shot uses the other hand, the walk flips screen direction, or the gesture completes twice.
The fix: match hand, speed, object, orientation; cut during the move, not after.

faq.q: What is Match on Action in film?
faq.a: Match on action is a cut made during one continuous gesture so movement bridges two camera positions. One side starts the action; the other side finishes it.

faq.q: Match on Action vs Match Cut
faq.a: Match on action stays inside one event and hides a change of view. A match cut joins two different images that correspond in form, space, sound, or idea.

faq.q: When should I use Match on Action?
faq.a: Use it when you need a new size or angle on the same ongoing move: a door, a hit, a sit. Do not use it to skip time or change location.

faq.q: How do I prompt Match on Action for AI image or video?
faq.a: Describe a gesture started in one framing and finished in the next. Name the hand, the object, and the cut during motion. Example: Match on action through [Subject]'s gesture, continuity glue.

title: Match Cut
narrative: One side of the join is complete. The other side is complete.
What they share is the point: a bone leaving a hand, then a craft in the same screen path; a match blown out, then a sun the same size in the frame. The splice is the sentence.

Use it when two images are the same idea and you want that idea to land in one frame of time. It is the wrong tool when you only need a new camera position on the same gesture: that job belongs to match on action , and forcing a rhyme will feel like decoration.
If the second image does not change what the first one meant, skip the trick. A contour rhyme with no conceptual load is a graphic match wearing a bigger name.
how: Design both frames as a pair before either is shot. Match the dominant contour, screen position, motion vector, or sonic envelope, then cut hard.
There is no optical mix: A is 100 percent, then B is 100 percent, and the correspondence is what the viewer supplies in the gap. Keep the shared property honest.

A door that sticks in the first shot must stick for the same mechanical reason later. Prompt both sides: name the outgoing object, the incoming object, the shared geometry or motion, and a hard cut, not a morph.
when: Use it at the leap: tool to tool, flame to sun, a planted object returning with a new meaning. Do not use it as a pretty way to leave a room.
If the next shot is only the next room, a straight cut or a Dissolve is cleaner.
vs: A graphic match rhymes form (shape, line, color, placement) even when the idea is thin. A match cut can use that rhyme, but it needs a correspondence of meaning, space, or sound as well.
Match on action stays inside one continuous gesture and hides the camera change. Match Motion rides a vector into another place or time.
Morph interpolates pixels; a match cut does not.
examples_film: In 2001: A Space Odyssey the thrown bone is followed by an orbiting craft on a related path, tool to tool across eras. In Lawrence of Arabia a blown match is followed by the desert sun at matching scale.
Apocalypse Now binds ceiling fan and helicopter so the two rotors share a thought. Use those joins as grammar, not as frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a morph or a graphic match with nothing to say. The tell is identical subject identity with no shared geometry, or a liquid melt from A into B.
The fix: lock the shared contour, placement, or motion; keep the two objects distinct; cut hard.

faq.q: What is Match Cut in film?
faq.a: A match cut is an edit that connects two complete shots through a visual, spatial, sonic, or conceptual correspondence. Both sides of the join are readable on their own; the splice is what claims they belong together.

faq.q: Match Cut vs Graphic Match
faq.a: A graphic match is a form rhyme: silhouette, circle, line, or color in the same screen place. A match cut may use that rhyme, but it also carries an idea, a space, or a sound from one side of the join to the other.

faq.q: When should I use Match Cut?
faq.a: Use it when two images are the same thought and the cut should make that thought visible. Do not use it to paper over a missing camera position on one action.

faq.q: How do I prompt Match Cut for AI image or video?
faq.a: Describe shot A, shot B, the shared shape or motion, and a hard cut. Example: Match cut from [Subject] to a rhyming shape in another time, bone to station. Say no morph and no dissolve.

title: Match Motion
narrative: A fall toward a mattress becomes a fall toward grass. A dive into a pool completes as a lunge onto a bed.
Hide the cut inside a vector. The body is the continuity; the room is allowed to lie.

Use it to carry someone through an impossible transition: dream to street, train to meadow, one chase into another. It is the wrong tool when you are still in the same room and only changing cameras on one gesture: that is Match on Action .

Matching only the actor's face, with no shared phase of motion, will not hide the leap. A whip can supply the blur that sells the vector ( Whip Pan ), but the match is the body's direction and speed, not the smear alone.
how: Match pose, screen position, camera angle, motion direction, and speed at the cut. Plan the two shots as a pair (or a shared rig).
Cut at a readable phase: mid-fall, mid-turn, mid-stride. The outgoing world and the incoming world can disagree; the vector must not.
Prompt: match-motion cut on [Subject], direction and speed continuing across the join so the cut rides the movement.
when: Use it to leave a dream, to stitch a chase across towns, to let a dance continue in another decade. Do not use it as ordinary coverage inside one hallway.
If the action is the same event, match on action. If only the contour matches and the body is still, use a Graphic Match or Match Cut .
vs: Match on Action is one continuous event, two views, same world. Match-motion can change the world if the vector holds.
A Whip Pan hides a cut in camera blur; match-motion hides it in subject motion (they can combine). A Match Cut may be still.
Invisible Cut conceals a splice in occlusion; the motion match is a visible, readable continuation.
examples_film: The Graduate connects pool and bedroom through Benjamin's movement so the body finishes what the water started. Paprika carries gestures between incompatible dream spaces.
Baby Driver rides motion from music and cars across joins. Lawrence of Arabia 's match-to-sun is more a still match cut; use it only if you are matching a rising gesture, not just a circle.
Borrow the vector, not the wardrobe.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Match on Action (same room) or a Match Cut of two stills. The tell: the walk resets, speed changes, or the subject is static on both sides.
The fix: match phase, direction, and speed; let geography jump; cut during the move.

faq.q: What is Match Motion in film?
faq.a: A match-motion cut continues direction and speed across the edit so the splice rides a vector. One side starts the movement; the other keeps it, even if place or reality changes.

faq.q: Match Motion vs Match on Action
faq.a: Match on action hides a camera change inside one continuous event in one world. Match motion can carry that event's vector into another location, time, or dream.

faq.q: When should I use Match Motion?
faq.a: Use it when a body should tow the viewer through an impossible change of world. Do not use it for ordinary coverage of one gesture in one room.

faq.q: How do I prompt Match Motion for AI image or video?
faq.a: Describe the same direction and speed on both sides, and name the world change. Example: Match-motion cut on [Subject], direction and speed continuing across the join. Hard cut, matched pose, no morph.

title: Match Split
narrative: A table edge runs from a 1960s kitchen into a present-day diner. A face is halved: left is the party you imagined, right is the party you got.
One line, two worlds. Use it when a split should feel like one organism rather than two televisions.

It is the wrong tool when the panes have no shared contour and are only simultaneous: that is ordinary Split Screen . It is also the wrong tool when you cut from one full frame to another rhyming full frame: that is a Match Cut or Graphic Match .
The divide is not a scratch. It is a designed seam that the eye can follow.
how: Compose both halves so a line, eyeline, horizon, or motion vector continues across the boundary. Match scale of heads if two versions of one person share a couch.
Keep lighting motivated per world unless the gag is that light also matches. Prompt: match split of [Subject], a graphic divide that continues a line or motion into another space.
when: Use it for twins, double lives, expectation versus reality, a road that is two times of day. Do not use it if the two spaces should not touch graphically.
If you need a phone call with frankly separate rooms, a clean split is enough.
vs: Split Screen co-presents; match split is a split whose form rhymes or continues. A Match Cut replaces one full image with another.
Frame within Frame is a window in the set. Graphic Match happens across a hard cut in time, not across a simultaneous seam.
examples_film: The Parent Trap seats two versions of one girl in a shared graphic so the split is a relationship. (500) Days of Summer divides a party into expectation and reality along a readable seam.
Use the continued line, not the plot.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a generic Split Screen with unmatched eyelines, or a Match Cut in sequence. The tell: two stacked clips with no shared line, or a cut instead of a co-present seam.
The fix: design the divide, continue one contour, hold both worlds at once.

faq.q: What is Match Split in film?
