faq.a: A match split is a divided frame where a line, motion, or contour continues from one world into the other. Both sides of the join are visible together and graphically related.

faq.q: Match Split vs Split Screen
faq.a: Split screen shows two fields at once. Match split is a split that rhymes or continues a line across the seam. All match splits are splits; not all splits match.

faq.q: When should I use Match Split?
faq.a: Use it when one contour should belong to two worlds at the same time. Do not use it for a simple phone-call panel with no shared geometry.

faq.q: How do I prompt Match Split for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the continued line and both halves. Example: Match split of [Subject], a graphic divide that continues a line or motion into another space. Simultaneous panes, no morph.

title: Montage
narrative: Workers, then a slaughterhouse. The cut is an argument.
Or: sweat, rope, steps, a breath, the same stairs later, a body that can now climb. Time has collapsed, and the sequence did the climbing.
Use it when you need months in a minute, or an idea neither image holds alone. It is the wrong tool when two ongoing actions must remain simultaneously alive: that is Cross-Cutting .
It is the wrong tool when you only want to skip a few seconds in one setup: that is a Jump Cut . An evocative analogy is not factual proof.
Do not let the sequence imply unsupported real-world causation.
how: State the intended inference or the time curve first. Choose images whose relation is legible: matching geometry for analogy, progressive sizes or sweat for training, repeated rituals for addiction.

Control duration as a metric (shortening toward a peak, or a held pause as payoff). Prompt: montage sequence built around [Subject], time collapsed by images, training, travel, or a life in twenty shots.
when: Use it for training, a marriage dying over breakfasts, a city arriving, an essay of images. Do not use it to cover a scene you could have played in continuity.
If the audience must follow one fight blow by blow, shoot the fight.
vs: Cross-Cutting braids parallel actions that continue. Montage often finishes each shot as a unit in an argument or a time-lapse of life.
Jump Cut holes out one setup. Fragments withhold a complete view of one event; montage may show complete views whose collision is the event.
Quick Cuts are a duration pattern; they become montage when the order makes a claim.
examples_film: Rocky and The Karate Kid compress training into progressive labor. Strike and October collide images into political argument.
Citizen Kane breakfasts a marriage down to silence. Up condenses a life into selected moments.
Steal the function (compress, argue), not the needle-drops.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Quick Cuts with no claim, or a single moving camera. The tell: twenty angles of the same five seconds, or a morphing collage.
The fix: pick an inference or a time span, choose distinct images, cut on order, let the join do the work.

faq.q: What is Montage in film?
faq.a: Montage is meaning or compression made by the order of shots. Each side of a join is a picture; the idea appears in the juxtaposition, not in either image alone.

faq.q: Montage vs Cross-Cutting
faq.a: Cross-cutting keeps two action lines running in implied simultaneity. Montage compresses duration or collides images to make a claim. One races clocks; the other builds an argument or a month.

faq.q: When should I use Montage?
faq.a: Use it when you need months in a minute, or an idea that only exists between images. Do not use it as a pile of unused coverage from one scene.

faq.q: How do I prompt Montage for AI image or video?
faq.a: List the shots and the claim. Example: Montage sequence built around [Subject], time collapsed by images, training, travel, or a life in twenty shots. Specify order, not a single moving take.

title: Quick Cuts
narrative: Eyes, hands, a kit, a face, the room, the stick, faster. You feel a release coming before the last hit lands.
Pace is the meaning. A sudden hold in that pattern can be the climax.

Use it when acceleration or a metric pulse should do narrative work: a showdown tightening from bodies to eyes, a raid, a practice that becomes punishment. It is the wrong tool when the similar frame is losing time: that is a Jump Cut .
It is the wrong tool when you are withholding the complete event in shards: that is Fragments . Faster is not always more tense.
Contrast between acceleration and a held pause often carries the payoff.
how: Design a duration curve and a progression of shot sizes. Alternate angles enough that each cut is a new view, not a hole in one view.
Use musical or physical accents selectively; not every splice must land on a beat. Prompt: quick cuts around [Subject], shots shorter than a breath, rhythm as violence or music.
when: Use it to tighten a duel, a performance, a chase through hands and gauges. Do not use it on a conversation that needs air.
If the pattern never rests, the last hit has nowhere to land.
vs: A Jump Cut is a skip inside a similar setup. A Crash Cut is one brutal join.

Montage may use short shots, but montage's job is collision of meaning or collapsed months; quick cuts' job is rate. Fragments hide the whole action; quick cuts often show the action in many complete, brief views.
examples_film: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly tightens the three-way showdown from bodies and positions toward faces and eyes. Whiplash binds image duration to pressure and rhythm.
Mad Max: Fury Road and Requiem for a Dream use short shots as pulse. Steal the curve, not the coverage plan.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Jump Cut (same frame, missing time) or chaos with no curve. The tell: every shot is the same length and size, or the camera never changes axis.
The fix: new views, shortening (or a designed break), a last image that can resolve the pulse.

faq.q: What is Quick Cuts in film?
faq.a: Quick cuts are a run of very short shots from changing setups, so duration becomes rhythm. Each side of a join is a new view; the rate is the meaning.

faq.q: Quick Cuts vs Jump Cut
faq.a: A jump cut skips time inside a similar framing. Quick cuts change angle, size, or subject every breath. One is a hole in a setup; the other is a metric pattern.

faq.q: When should I use Quick Cuts?
faq.a: Use it when pace should tighten a duel, a performance, or a chase. Do not use it as default coverage, and do not confuse it with a jump inside one frame.

faq.q: How do I prompt Quick Cuts for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for many short, distinct shots and a duration curve. Example: Quick cuts around [Subject], shots shorter than a breath, rhythm as violence or music. Name the progression of sizes.

title: Set Transition
narrative: A dressing room wall slides and you are in a nightclub. A theatre door is a street.
Geography itself edits. The subject may not have cut; the world did.

Use it when the story's spaces are porous: backstage as mind, city as stage, a lobby that rewrites under fire. It is the wrong tool when you only need to hide a splice in a whip: that is an Invisible Cut .
It is the wrong tool when A melts into B as a picture: that is Morphing . If the camera passes through a wall into another place as a portal gag, you are next to Pass Through .
Set transition is the room changing around the body.
how: Build two (or more) complete spaces that can physically or digitally replace each other on a continuous move: sliding flats, revolving walls, a stitch on a doorway, a digital set extension that rewrites. Keep lighting motivated as the space changes, or let the lights change as part of the trick.

Prompt: set transition around [Subject], the location transforming in camera, walls walking, one space becoming another. Motion brief: the set around [Subject] transforms into a new location without a hard cut.
when: Use it to walk from rehearsal into performance, from memory into a street, from one building into another without admitting an edit. Do not use it if a hard cut or a wipe would tell the truth faster.
Virtuosity with nothing new in the second space is empty.
vs: An Invisible Cut conceals a splice; the set may stay the same. A Pass Through drives the camera through a surface into another space.
Morphing interpolates the image. A set transition rewrites architecture along a continuous path, theatrical or digital.
Match Motion can change worlds on a body vector without the walls walking.
examples_film: Birdman lets theatre and city feel like one porous set. 1917 hides joins so trenches, ruins, and fields play as continuous geography.
The Matrix lobby rewrites a space through action and spatial continuity. Use the porous building, not a copied tracking path.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Morphing the actor, or a visible cut in a doorway. The tell: the person melts, or there is a pop at the threshold.
The fix: keep the body continuous, let walls or set extension rewrite, hide or omit the splice, match lighting across the change.

faq.q: What is Set Transition in film?
faq.a: A set transition changes location in camera as architecture rewrites around the subject. Both sides of the join are places on one continuous path, not two shots with a hard cut.

faq.q: Set Transition vs Invisible Cut
faq.a: An invisible cut hides an edit; the set might not change. A set transition makes geography the edit: walls walk, rooms become other rooms. One conceals a splice; the other rewrites space.

faq.q: When should I use Set Transition?
faq.a: Use it when spaces should feel porous and the camera should not admit a cut. Do not use it as a flex when a straight scene change would be clearer.

faq.q: How do I prompt Set Transition for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name both locations and a continuous camera. Example: Set transition around [Subject], walls walking, one space becoming another. Video: the set transforms without a hard cut. Keep the body stable.

title: Smash Cut
narrative: A night walk tightens. A bus door hisses into the frame.
The scare was a vehicle, not a monster, and the cut is the joke and the slap at once. Or: a grave visit settles, then a hand breaks the earth.
The next image should hurt. Use it when contrast is the meaning.
It is the wrong tool when the two sides are similar, or when you still need the audience inside one continuous action. Similar frames with missing time are a Jump Cut .
A few stolen frames of another image are a Flash Cut . Earn the first state.
A smash from nowhere, with no quiet or no prayer, is only loud.
how: Hold A long enough to establish tone, scale, or apparent closure. Cut to B with a large change in brightness, loudness, shot size, or subject class: silence to noise, interior to blast, hymn to murder.

No dissolve, no fade, no matched contour unless the match is itself the insult. Coordinate picture and sound so they smash together, or delay the sound for a second smash (the blast seen, then heard).
Prompt: from [Subject] to a violently different image, no polite dissolve.
when: Use it at the false ending, the bus in the dark, the cut from a kiss to a siren. Do not use it on every scene change.
If nothing in A was quiet, sacred, or resolved, B has nothing to smash.
vs: A Jump Cut stays in a similar frame and skips time. A Crash Cut is a hard collision used as percussion or as a start inside an event; smash cut is contrast after a state has been earned.
A Match Cut rhymes; smash cut usually refuses the rhyme. Cross-Cutting alternates lines over time; smash is one brutal join.
examples_film: Cat People uses the bus to interrupt a tense walk: the cut is the scare and its release. Carrie lets the aftermath settle, then destabilizes the coda.
Whiplash smashes quiet into the kit. Oppenheimer lets the Trinity flash arrive before the blast sound.
Contrast as grammar, not a shot to duplicate.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Dissolve (polite) or a Jump Cut (same setup). The tell: A and B have similar brightness, scale, and tone, so nothing smashes.
The fix: earn a state on A, change at least two axes (sound and scale, or tone and time) on B, cut hard.

faq.q: What is Smash Cut in film?
faq.a: A smash cut is an abrupt, high-contrast join in image, sound, tone, scale, or time. One side of the splice has a state; the other side breaks it without a blend.

faq.q: Smash Cut vs Jump Cut
faq.a: A jump cut skips time inside a similar framing. A smash cut leaves that world for a violently different one. Similarity is the jump cut's tell; contrast is the smash cut's tell.

faq.q: When should I use Smash Cut?
faq.a: Use it when the next image should hurt after quiet, prayer, or false closure. Do not use it as a default scene change.

faq.q: How do I prompt Smash Cut for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the earned state and the contradicting image. Example: Smash cut from [Subject] to a violently different image, silence to noise, no dissolve. Hold A, then hard-cut to B.

title: Split Screen
narrative: A phone call places two apartments in one picture. A party splits into the night you wanted and the night you got.
Dual identity, dual time, or dual witness: the pane is the grammar. Use it when two rooms must be one moment, or when comparison is the joke.
It is the wrong tool when the audience should assume contact and then be wrong: that surprise is often better as Cross-Cutting . It is also not a window, doorway, or mirror inside the set.
That is Frame within Frame , a diegetic frame, not a panel. Replaying an event from another angle does not automatically make the accounts unreliable.
Split screen can show agreement as easily as a lie.
how: Shoot or generate each pane with matched eye-lines, horizon, or motion if you want the split to feel like one organism (a Match Split ). Or keep the panes frankly separate for a phone call.
Decide the boundary: hard vertical, architectural, torn. Keep identity stable unless the point is two versions of one person.
Prompt: split screen with [Subject] in one pane and another life in the other, simultaneous spaces, phone-call cinema or dual identity.
when: Use it for simultaneous phone calls, twins, expectation versus reality, four quadrants of one hour. Do not use it as wallpaper on a single conversation that wants ordinary coverage.
If you need the second room later, cut later.
vs: Cross-Cutting alternates; split screen co-presents. Frame within Frame is a picture found in the world (a window, a phone, a doorway).
Match Split is a split whose dividing line or contour continues from one world into the other. Montage sequences images; split screen stacks them now.
examples_film: Pillow Talk and other studio comedies park two ends of a phone call in one frame. Timecode runs four continuous views in quadrants.
Kill Bill and Sisters use panels as simultaneous action. (500) Days of Summer splits expectation and reality at a party.
Use the pane logic, not a copied poster.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Frame within Frame (a real window) or Cross-Cutting (sequential). The tell: a doorway in the set, or the model giving you one wide with a scratch down the middle.
The fix: two fully directed spaces, a graphic divide, simultaneous time.

faq.q: What is Split Screen in film?
faq.a: Split screen shows multiple image fields at once. Both sides of the join occupy the frame together, so two rooms or two versions share one moment.

faq.q: Split Screen vs Cross-Cutting
faq.a: Cross-cutting alternates lines so you see one, then the other. Split screen presents them simultaneously. Alternation creates meanwhile; panels create co-presence.

faq.q: When should I use Split Screen?
faq.a: Use it when two spaces must be one moment: a call, twins, expectation versus reality. Do not use it as a substitute for a window in the set or for ordinary coverage.

faq.q: How do I prompt Split Screen for AI image or video?
faq.a: Describe each pane and the divide. Example: Split screen with [Subject] in one pane and another life in the other, simultaneous spaces. Specify a hard boundary and two complete scenes.

title: Transitions
narrative: A wipe turns a page. A match claims an idea.
A dissolve remembers. A whip throws you.
The cut should be seen. This is the parent of those gestures, not a substitute for choosing one.
Use it when invisible continuity would lie, or when the join is the joke, the thesis, or the chapter mark. It is the wrong tool when the scene should feel found and unedited.
Then hide the cut, or do not cut. Pick a species.
'A cool transition' is not a shot list. Name wipe, match, mix, light, or whip.
how: Decide what the join must do: rhyme ( Match Cut ), mix ( Dissolve ), empty ( Fade In / Fade Out ), travel an edge ( Wipe ), point ( Iris ), blur ( Whip Pan ), or rewrite space ( Set Transition ). Design A and B together so the chosen gesture has material to work with.
Prompt: a designed transition around [Subject], the join as a gesture: wipe, morph, match, or light.
when: Use it at act breaks, world leaps, jokes about cinema, or any time the how of leaving matters. Do not use a designed transition on every reverse in a talk scene.
If nothing in the story changes at the splice except the camera, a straight cut is the design.
vs: A Match Cut is a correspondence across a hard cut. A Dissolve is a mix.
A Whip Pan can hide or announce a join through blur. A Wipe shows a traveling edge.
This page is the choice to make the join a gesture; those pages are the species. Invisible Cut is the opposing doctrine.
examples_film: Star Wars makes scene changes into directional wipes, a serial grammar. 2001: A Space Odyssey makes a hard match the largest leap in the film.
Use them as proof that a visible join can carry story, not as a kit to paste on every cut.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is an Invisible Cut you accidentally made visible, or a morph used because no join was chosen. The tell: A and B have no designed relationship, and a filter slurries them.
The fix: pick a species, give both sides a job, execute that physics only.

faq.q: What is Transitions in film?
faq.a: Transitions in this sense are designed joins, splices the audience is meant to notice. Both sides of the join are planned as a pair, and the gesture (wipe, match, mix, light) is part of the sentence.

faq.q: Transitions vs Match Cut
faq.a: A match cut is one species of designed join: correspondence across a hard cut. Transitions as a heading means choosing a visible gesture at all, which might be a match, a wipe, a dissolve, or a whip.

faq.q: When should I use Transitions?
faq.a: Use a designed transition when the how of leaving A is story. Do not decorate every reverse. If the join should vanish, do not design it as a gesture.

faq.q: How do I prompt Transitions for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name A, B, and the species of join. Example: a designed transition around [Subject], the join as a gesture: wipe, morph, match, or light. Forbid vague words like seamless or cool.

title: Wipe
narrative: A vertical line walks left to right and a village becomes a mountain pass. Geography has changed as a page turn, not as an invisible cut.
Adventure, serials, and playful maps like that honesty. Use it when the change of scene should feel brisk, storybook, or openly constructed.
It is the wrong tool when you need the audience not to feel an edit: that is Invisible Cut or Match on Action . A wipe is not a person walking in front of the lens (occlusion).
Occlusion can hide a cut; a wipe displays one. Direction and speed should agree with the next action.
A wipe against the traveler's walk fights the grammar.
how: Choose a boundary: vertical, horizontal, diagonal, clock hand, barn-door, shape. Animate it across a clean pair of shots.

Soft-edged or hard-edged is a taste choice; the edge must remain a graphic, not a morph of the scenery. A motivated object edge (a passing wall, a cloak) can justify a wipe, but then you are close to an invisible occlusion cut.
Prompt: wipe replacing [Subject] with the next image, a line traveling across the frame, a clock hand or a hard vertical.
when: Use it to leap from planet to planet, village to road, chapter to chapter in a serial cadence. Do not use it to hide a continuity error.
If the join should vanish, do not wipe.
vs: An Iris is a radial mask from a center, not a traveling edge. A Match Cut rhymes two full frames with a hard cut and no boundary.
A Dissolve mixes opacities. An Invisible Cut uses a real object or blur to conceal the splice; the wipe's graphic boundary is intentional and visible.
examples_film: Star Wars uses directional wipes as adventure punctuation between locations. Seven Samurai uses wipes to mark narrative progression with a visible page-turn.
Those are grammar samples for an honest scene change, not compositions to clone.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is an Invisible Cut (hidden occlusion) or a Dissolve . The tell: the edge is gooey, or a passing extra is doing the work while you call it a wipe.
The fix: a clean traveling mask, two intact pictures, direction matched to the story's travel.

faq.q: What is Wipe in film?
faq.a: A wipe replaces one shot with another through a moving boundary across the screen. Both sides of the join are full pictures; the traveling edge is the edit, and it is meant to be seen.

faq.q: Wipe vs Iris
faq.a: A wipe's edge travels (left to right, clock, barn-door). An iris is a circular or shaped mask that opens or closes around a center. One is a page turn; the other is a pointing hole.

faq.q: When should I use Wipe?
faq.a: Use it for adventure, serial geography, or a playful scene change that should not pretend to be invisible. Do not use it to hide a splice the audience must not feel.

faq.q: How do I prompt Wipe for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name both images and the traveling edge. Example: Wipe replacing [Subject] with the next image, a line traveling across the frame. Specify direction and a clean mask, not a morph.

title: Altered State
narrative: Edges trail. Hue unhooks from the room.
A face leaves a stain. Focus and speed refuse to sit still.
The set may be an apartment. The picture is a nervous system.
Use it when perception is the plot: drugs, vertigo, dying, revelation. Pick a few physical tells and repeat them so the state has rules.
A smear plus a color unhook is a language. Everything at once is noise.
It is the wrong tool for a single clean optic (one fisheye, one flare) that the character would still recognize as the room. If the codec collapses, that is datamosh.
If two times overlay as density, that is double exposure. Altered state may borrow those, but it has to be motivated as seeing.
how: Combine a short list: long shutter smear, step-printed time, wrong white balance, afterimages, a diopter or a distorting optic, occasional overlay. Keep the body of the subject readable enough to stay in the scene.
Prompt: perception bent, edges trailing, color unhooked from the room, as if consciousness is slipping, not a random glitch pack.
when: A close interior where the frame warps as a character slips, trailing edges, hue wrong, time sticky. Do not apply it to a wide establishing shot that still has to map the street.
vs: Dreamcore is a genre look of liminal rooms and childhood lighting gone wrong. Altered state is the perceptual event, often in an ordinary set.
Datamosh is codec collapse. Double Exposure is a stacked record.
Distortions are geometric lies in the glass. Altered state may include distortion, plus time and color that will not sit.
examples_film: Enter the Void binds camera, smear, and color to a consciousness that will not stay in a body. Requiem for a Dream uses speed, close optics, and cutting as intoxication and crash.
Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas is the wide-angle, wrong-color cousin.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: a single fisheye, a datamosh, or a dreamcore bedroom with no perceptual event. Tell: a clean room with one sticker effect, or total illegibility.
Fix: motivate two or three repeating tells, keep the subject locatable, let the room remain a room that is failing.

faq.q: What is altered state in film?
faq.a: Subjective photography in which smear, afterimage, color, and time report a mind rather than a sober room. It is a motivated bundle, not one optic.

faq.q: Altered state vs distortions
faq.a: Distortions are geometric warps from glass or air. Altered state may use those, plus color and time errors, as consciousness. Distortion can be sober (a peephole). Altered state is not.

faq.q: When should I use altered state?
faq.a: When the mind is the location. Do not use it as decoration on coverage that still has to be geographically clear.

faq.q: How do I prompt altered state for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name two or three tells (trail, afterimage, wrong hue, sticky time) and say consciousness is slipping. Forbid a generic glitch overlay and keep the subject readable.

title: Anamorphic Flare
narrative: Night lamps and headlights write a bar across the frame because the front optic stretches one axis. The streak is cyan, blue, or magenta depending on coatings, and it stays level with the squeezed world.
Oval highlights in the background confirm the same glass. Use it when the night should be written on the taking lens: wet streets, neon, a car coming toward camera.
The streak is evidence of scope optics, not of brightness alone. It is the wrong tool in spherical coverage, or when you want a circular ghost of the iris.
If the bokeh is round and the streak is a random rainbow, you have mixed two lens families.
how: Shoot anamorphic (typically 2x squeeze). Put a hard point source in or near frame: headlight, practical, sun.
Keep the cylindrical axis consistent so streaks stay horizontal. Coatings and the front element decide color and length.
Stop down and ovals become more polygonal. In a prompt, say horizontal anamorphic streak, name the hue, and demand oval bokeh, not round discs.
when: A car cresting a wet overpass at night, headlights drawing cyan bars through a figure in a raincoat. Do not add horizontal streaks to a spherical 50mm close-up with round bokeh.
vs: Lens Flare covers ghosts, veiling, and spherical scatter. Anamorphic flare is the horizontal bar from cylindrical glass.
Anamorphic is the lens format itself: squeeze, oval bokeh, and the flare are consequences. Bokeh is the out-of-focus disc shape.
Oval discs support the claim. Round discs contradict it.
examples_film: Blade Runner lets neon and headlights write on anamorphic glass. J.
Abrams films push the horizontal streak until it becomes a signature. Super 8 (2011) uses the same family of bars as period scope language.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: generic lens flare or a spherical rainbow. Tell: round bokeh with a pasted horizontal bar that ignores source position.
Fix: match oval highlights, keep streaks horizontal, and lock them to a pictured point source.

faq.q: What is anamorphic flare in film?
faq.a: A horizontal streak from light hitting cylindrical anamorphic elements. It is optical, usually paired with oval bokeh from the same squeeze.

faq.q: Anamorphic flare vs lens flare
faq.a: Lens flare is any scatter in the optic. Anamorphic flare is specifically the long horizontal bar of squeezed glass, not circular ghosts or a general veil.

faq.q: When should I use anamorphic flare?
faq.a: When night points (headlights, neon, practicals) should write on scope glass. Do not use it on spherical lenses with round bokeh.

faq.q: How do I prompt anamorphic flare for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for horizontal streaks, a named hue, oval bokeh, and a point source in or near frame. Ban round discs and floating rainbows.

title: Anthropo
narrative: A red balloon waits, follows, sulks. A robot tilts its head at a trash cube.
The object is not a prop in a still life. It is covered like a person: singles, looks, pauses.
Will is implied by blocking and eyeline, not by a drawn smile unless the story needs one. Use it to give a thing agency: a balloon, a machine, a relic, an animal shot as a colleague.

The rest of the scene should treat it as a presence. It is the wrong tool when you simply shoot an object from its own optical position (that is object POV) or when a tableau arranges bodies as a picture.
Anthropo is performance coverage of a nonhuman. Object POV is a camera mount.
how: Assign an eyeline height. Cover the object with the same sizes you would give an actor: wide for entrance, medium for dialogue, close for reaction.
Let humans look at it as a partner. Puppet, wire, or animation can supply gesture.
Prompt: an object or animal given human scale, gesture, or eyeline, the inanimate performing, not a POV from inside the object.
when: A balloon at head height, held in a single, a child looking to it as if it might answer. Do not bolt the camera to the balloon and call that anthropo.
That is object POV.
vs: Object POV puts the camera in the object's position. Anthropo looks at the object as an actor.
Tableau freezes people into a composed picture. Anthropo keeps a will in motion.
Macro can isolate an object as texture without giving it an eyeline.
examples_film: The Red Balloon covers a balloon as a companion, with waits and follows that belong to a performer. WALL-E plays a machine with human gesture and eyeline without needing a human face.
Those are coverage choices, not mascots to copy.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: object POV, a cute sticker face, or a still-life insert. Tell: the camera is mounted in the object, or the object sits as a prop with no eyeline.
Fix: assign a look, a height, and reaction coverage. Let others treat it as a partner.

faq.q: What is anthropo in film?
faq.a: Staging and covering an object or animal as if it were a performer: scale, gesture, eyeline, reactions. Agency is in the blocking, not necessarily in a painted face.

faq.q: Anthropo vs object POV
faq.a: Object POV is the camera from the thing's position. Anthropo is the camera looking at the thing as an actor. One is a mount. The other is a performance.

faq.q: When should I use anthropo?
faq.a: When a nonhuman should have a will in the scene. Do not use it for a mere product insert or for a true POV from inside the object.

faq.q: How do I prompt anthropo for AI image or video?
faq.a: Specify human scale, a clear eyeline, gesture, and coverage as if the object were a player. Forbid interior POV unless you want that cousin.

title: Argus
narrative: Surveillance becomes anatomy. A wall of cameras.
A god covered in irises. Use it when paranoia, divinity, or the internet should be visible as too much seeing.
It is the wrong tool for a single honest portrait, and for a tidy split of two scenes. If the same person repeats as clones, that is duplication.
If the frame is divided into panels, that is split screen. If facets mirror one image, that is a kaleidoscope.
how: Count the eyes. Place them as objects: on skin, on walls, as a field of viewpoints around a still center.
Keep a readable subject so the swarm has a king. Light each iris with a small catchlight if they are organs.
If they are cameras, give each lens a tiny practical. Do not dissolve them into noise.
Prompt an Argus image of the subject: many eyes, many viewpoints, a creature or a city of looking.
when: Use it for paranoia, gods, a network that stares. Do not use it as extra pupils on a portrait that only needed one pair.
vs: Duplication repeats a person. Argus multiplies looking, not necessarily the whole body.
Split Screen divides the frame into panels of action. Argus can be one composition swarming with eyes.
Kaleidoscope mirrors facets. Here the eyes are the point.
examples_film: Doctor Strange kaleidoscopes tunnel looking into too many angles. The Fountain multiplies visionary sight.
Grammar of a swarm of gazes, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is flare on a face, or a Split Screen . The tell is no extra eyes as objects, or a tidy two-way divide.
The fix is countable pupils or viewpoints, a swarm with a center.

faq.q: What is Argus in film?
faq.a: Argus is many eyes and many viewpoints: a creature or a city of looking. One gaze is not enough. Looking becomes a swarm.

faq.q: Argus vs duplication
faq.a: Duplication repeats a person in the frame. Argus multiplies eyes or viewpoints. You may still have one body. The surplus is seeing.

faq.q: When should I use Argus?
faq.a: Use it for paranoia, gods, networks of watching. Skip it on a single honest portrait, and skip it when you only need two panels of action.

faq.q: How do I prompt Argus for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Argus image of [Subject], many eyes, many viewpoints. Count them. Keep a center so it is not noise. Eyes should be objects, not flare.

title: Bokeh
narrative: A city, a string of practicals, or a wet street becomes a field of discs. Circular blades make circles.
Anamorphic squeeze makes ovals. Mechanical vignetting cats-eyes the discs at the frame edge.
Nervous, outlined, or onion-ring discs are also bokeh. They are just unkind bokeh.
Use it when the world behind or in front of a face should become light rather than information. One plane stays true.
The rest is the optic's handwriting. It is the wrong tool when you need the room.
If background signs, eyelines, or geography still have to read, creamy discs are hiding the scene. It is also the wrong word for a masked cutout with no optical discs at all.
how: Open the aperture, separate subject from background, and choose glass: spherical circles, anamorphic ovals, Petzval swirl, cat-eye at the edges. Point sources (practicals, speculars, rain catches) make the discs visible.
Distance and focal length set disc size. Prompt the disc shape and the source of the highlights, not blurry background alone.
when: A close portrait in a cramped apartment, amber lamps and a magenta neon turning into circular or oval discs while the near eye stays sharp. Do not melt a wide master that still has blocking to read.
vs: Shallow Focus is the thin sharp plane. Bokeh is the look of whatever is off that plane.
Anamorphic turns those discs into ovals and often adds streaks. Rack Focus moves the sharp plane during the shot.
Bokeh can change as focus moves, but the pull is a different verb.
examples_film: In the Mood for Love turns crowded Hong Kong lamps into soft discs around faces. Her isolates Theodore against city lights whose character is the glass, not a painted smear.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: a cutout mask or generic shallow focus with no disc structure. Tell: hair cut out like a sticker, no specular discs, background replaced rather than optically soft.
Fix: keep optical discs, cat-eye at edges if wide open, and a real distance between planes.

faq.q: What is bokeh in film?
faq.a: The character of out-of-focus rendering: circles, ovals, cat-eyes, swirl, onion rings. It describes how blur looks, not merely that something is soft.

faq.q: Bokeh vs shallow focus
faq.a: Shallow focus is a narrow depth of field. Bokeh is the optical handwriting of that blur. You can have shallow focus with ugly bokeh.

faq.q: When should I use bokeh?
faq.a: When only one plane may be true and the rest should become light. Do not use it when the background still has to carry information.

faq.q: How do I prompt bokeh for AI image or video?
faq.a: Specify circular or oval discs, name the highlight sources, keep the subject sharp, and forbid cutout edges or a smeared backdrop.

title: Bubbles
narrative: A face repeats in a drifting sphere. Joy or threat depends on the light.
Use it when the air should be glass, cheap optics that still photograph. It is the wrong tool for a boardroom, and for sparks that have no film surface.
If the bits are solid motes, you want particles. If the picture is a mirror or a wet street, you want reflections on a plane.
how: Backlight or side-light soap films so each sphere shows a highlight and a refraction of the face. Keep surfaces: thin-film color at the edge, a wet tick.
The subject remains readable through the swarm. Shallow space helps.
Do not replace bubbles with out-of-focus lamps. Prompt bubbles around the subject: refraction worlds that still read as joy or threat.
Name soap or air bubbles, not bokeh.
when: Use it for joy, drowning, a spell, an underwater breath. Do not use it as fake bokeh on a night street with no soap films.
vs: Particles are solid, countable motes: dust, sparks, pollen. Bubbles have surfaces and refraction.
Reflections are images on glass, water, or chrome planes. A bubble is a tiny closed optic in the air.
examples_film: The Shape of Water lets water optics and drifting spheres share space with a body. Music videos use soap-film refraction as a lyric field.
Grammar of air as glass, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Bokeh disks or a particle mist. The tell is circles with no surface, no refraction, no wet edge.
The fix is soap films as little lenses, highlights on a skin of air.

faq.q: What is bubbles in film?
faq.a: Bubbles are little lenses in the air: soap films that refract the subject, with rainbow edges and wet highlights. Each one is an optic, not a blur disk.

faq.q: Bubbles vs particles
faq.a: Particles are solid bits. Bubbles have a film surface and refraction. One you could sweep up. The other is a sphere of air with a wet skin.

faq.q: When should I use bubbles?
faq.a: Use them when the air should be glass: joy, drowning, a spell. Skip them in a dry room that only needs dust, and skip fake bokeh.

faq.q: How do I prompt bubbles for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Bubbles around [Subject], refraction worlds. Demand soap-film surfaces, rainbow edges, and the face repeating in the spheres. Do not ask for bokeh lamps.

title: Chromatic Aberration
narrative: Cheap, wide, or vintage glass fails to put all colors on the same plane. A branch, a shoulder, a neon sign grows a red or cyan beard.
The optic is imperfect on purpose, or it is simply old. Use it when the glass should confess: lo-fi night, a dream that is optical rather than a grade, a wide at full aperture.
Tie fringes to contrast edges, stronger in the corners. It is the wrong tool as a full-frame RGB split, which is a channel offset, not aberration.
If the whole image is three layers of the same picture, you have a digital treatment, not CA.
how: Wide angle, wide open, simple or vintage designs. Lateral CA scales with distance from center.
Longitudinal CA shows as color bokeh (magenta in front, green behind, or the reverse). Recreate by fringing high-contrast edges, not by sliding entire channels.
Prompt: red-cyan fringing at high-contrast edges, stronger at the frame edge, cheap or vintage glass.
when: A night overpass, raincoat against neon, red-cyan fringes on the brightest sign edges and the silhouette. Do not RGB-split the entire figure as if it were a channel offset.
vs: Lens Flare is scatter and ghosts, not edge fringes. Fisheye is extreme barrel distortion.
It can carry CA but is a geometry, not a color error. Vintage Cine Glass often includes CA plus haze and vignette.
Distortions are spatial warps. CA is a color-focus error on top of, or instead of, those warps.
examples_film: Spring Breakers lets cheap-looking fringing and analog error sit on party lights. Music videos often push lateral CA as a wide-open night look.
Enter the Void uses optical error as subjective night, which is grammar, not a template.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: RGB split, lens flare, or fisheye stretch. Tell: the whole subject is three colored copies, or only a rainbow streak with no edge fringe.
Fix: confine color to high-contrast edges, increase it off center, keep the core image registered.

faq.q: What is chromatic aberration in film?
faq.a: Color fringing from wavelengths that do not share a focus or a magnification. Lateral CA beards edges. Longitudinal CA colors the blur in front of and behind the mark.

faq.q: Chromatic aberration vs lens flare
faq.a: Flare is stray light making ghosts and veils. Chromatic aberration is a focusing error that puts different colors on contrast edges. One is scatter. The other is dispersion.

faq.q: When should I use chromatic aberration?
faq.a: When the optic should look imperfect: vintage glass, wide night work, a slightly untrustworthy image. Do not use a full-frame channel split.

faq.q: How do I prompt chromatic aberration for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for red-cyan (or named) fringing on high-contrast edges, stronger at the corners, from cheap or vintage glass. Ban whole-image RGB offsets.

title: Cinemagraph
narrative: The picture looks dead, then a kettle breathes. A coat is still.
Only the rain tracks the window. Time is allowed in one masked region.
The rest is a still. Use it when a photograph should refuse to fully stop: fashion, a poster that lives, a memory with one leak of motion.
The moving part must be plausible as a cycle. It is the wrong tool when the whole scene moves, or when all motion stops (freeze-frame).
If every element loops, that is an infinite loop of a shot, not a cinemagraph. If the loop is a boomerang of the entire take, that is a different toy.
how: Shoot a locked camera. Choose one motion that can cycle (steam, rain, flicker).
Mask that region in post, freeze the rest from a single frame, loop the live patch so the join is invisible. Prompt: almost a still, only one named element loops, locked camera, no other motion.
when: A woman at a rain window, body frozen, only the rain and a thread of steam looping. Do not let her blink, the curtains blow, and the neon flicker all at once.
vs: Freeze Frame stops everything. Infinite Loop repeats the entire shot.
Boomerang plays a whole action forward and back. A cinemagraph freezes the majority and loops a patch.
Time-Lapse advances the whole world in steps.
examples_film: The form comes from fashion stills (Jamie Beck and Kevin Burg) and advertising, not from a single feature grammar. Fashion films and window displays are the well-known uses: one living detail in a still.
La Jetee is a cousin of stills and motion, not a cinemagraph loop.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: freeze-frame, full-shot loop, or a normal live take. Tell: several motions alive, a visible loop bump, or a frozen frame with no live patch.
Fix: one masked element, invisible join, everything else from a single still.

faq.q: What is a cinemagraph in film?
faq.a: A still image with one isolated looping motion. The rest is frozen. It sits between a photograph and a clip.

faq.q: Cinemagraph vs freeze-frame
faq.a: A freeze-frame stops all motion. A cinemagraph stops almost all motion and keeps one element alive on a loop.

faq.q: When should I use a cinemagraph?
faq.a: When a still should have one living detail: steam, rain, a flicker. Do not use it if the whole scene needs to play, or if nothing should move.

faq.q: How do I prompt a cinemagraph for AI image or video?
faq.a: Say almost still, locked camera, and name the single looping element. Forbid additional motion and a visible loop cut.

title: Collage
narrative: A head from one still, a building from another, newsprint, a painted sky. You can see the scissors.
Mixed grain, mixed contrast, maybe a bit of tape. One image was not enough, so the frame was assembled.

Use it when sources should remain sources: titles, satire, memory as scrapbook, a graphic sequence that refuses photographic unity. It is the wrong tool when two photographs should fuse as density (double exposure) or when live action and animation share a photographed space without torn edges.
Mixed media can do either. Collage insists on the cut.
how: Shoot or collect plates. Cut them.
Leave borders, torn fiber, misregistered printing, different grain structures. Composite with hard or torn masks, not a screen blend.
Prompt: torn layers, mixed stocks, cut paper and live action sharing one plane, visible joins, not a smooth double exposure.
when: A portrait built from a live face, a city fragment, and newsprint, joins visible. Do not dissolve the same elements into a ghosted overlay and call it collage.
vs: Double Exposure is an optical or additive stack without scissors. Mixed Media is the broader family (animation plus live, print plus plate).
Collage is the cut-and-paste grammar inside that family. Split Screen divides the frame into simultaneous pictures with a designed border, usually live.
Collage can ignore a shared timebase.
examples_film: Terry Gilliam's Monty Python work is cut-out collage in motion. The Jinx titles treat documents and images as a stacked graphic plane.
Bruce Conner's A Movie is found-footage collage as a film, which is grammar for the cut, not a look to clone.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: double exposure or a clean split-screen. Tell: translucent blend, matching grain across pieces, or a hard live divider without paper or tear.
Fix: mismatched stocks, torn or cut borders, graphic stacking.

faq.q: What is collage in film?
faq.a: A frame assembled from cut or torn pieces of different images and materials, with joins meant to be seen. It is construction, not a seamless composite.

faq.q: Collage vs double exposure
faq.a: Double exposure blends records as density. Collage keeps edges: scissors, paper, mixed stocks. One is optical stack. The other is cut and paste.

faq.q: When should I use collage?
faq.a: When one photograph is not enough and the sources should stay visible. Do not use it for a ghosted memory overlay or a seamless twin shot.

faq.q: How do I prompt collage for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for torn layers, mixed film stocks or paper, live action plus cut pieces, and visible joins. Ban smooth double exposure.

title: Cyclope
narrative: A machine stares. A lighthouse stares.
A god stares. Distortion is the character.
The subject looms, edges fall away, a catchlight keeps the hole an organ. It is the wrong tool for a beauty close-up, and for a human point of view with hands in frame.
If you only want extreme wide geometry, use a fisheye as a lens. If a body owns the camera, that is first-person.
how: Write an extreme fisheye or a circular iris mask. Place the subject near the glass so the nose or the machine fills the hole.
Edges barrel. Keep one catchlight.
Do not add a Dutch unless the creature is off its axis. The camera is the eye.
Height is the creature's height, often slightly high or dead-on. Prompt a cyclope view: a single giant iris, fisheye as a monster eye, one hole looking.
when: Use it for surveillance, monsters, HAL-like machines, a stare that is not human. Do not use it on a portrait that still needs courtesy.
vs: Fisheye is the optic without the monster-eye mask: a wide, barrelled world. Cyclope is that optic as one organ.
First-Person implies a human body, hands, breath. Cyclope is a single hole that looks.
examples_film: 2001 's HAL is a red iris that watches. The Lighthouse turns a stare into a blinding organ.
Grammar of one eye, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a mildly wide close-up. The tell is a normal nose and a rectangular room.
The fix is a mountain of a near feature, a globe of a room, one iris.

faq.q: What is cyclope in film?
faq.a: Cyclope is a single giant iris looking, fisheye as a monster eye. The camera is one hole, too close, and distortion is the character.

faq.q: Cyclope vs fisheye
faq.a: Fisheye is a lens choice that barrels the world. Cyclope uses that distortion as a creature or machine eye, often with a circular hole and a catchlight.

faq.q: When should I use cyclope?
faq.a: Use it for a nonhuman stare: surveillance, monsters, a machine. Skip it for a flattering close-up or a human POV with hands.

faq.q: How do I prompt cyclope for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Cyclope view of [Subject], a single giant iris, fisheye as a monster eye, one hole looking. Demand barrel distortion and a catchlight. Keep one eye.

title: Datamosh
narrative: The I-frame never arrives. P-frames keep describing motion that no longer has a valid picture.
A mouth stretches into a wall. A cut happens in time but not in pixels.
Digital ruin is the style. Use it when the file should break on purpose: a music video, a corrupted memory, a broadcast that fails.

The smear should follow motion vectors, not a random RGB offset. It is the wrong tool for a stutter of whole frames (that is stop-stutter), for chromatic fringing, or for an altered-state smear from a long shutter.
If the image trails because the shutter was open, that is photography. If it trails because the codec predicted the wrong future, that is datamosh.
how: Encode with inter-frame compression, drop or repeat I-frames, let P-frames or B-frames run. The artifact is temporal and blocky, often with residual macroblocks.
Prompt: inter-frame collapse, faces smearing into the next GOP, codec wreckage, not RGB split, not film smear.
when: A cut from a face to a city in which the face's pixels are dragged across the skyline by leftover motion vectors. Do not step-print the same clip or add red-cyan edge fringe and call it datamosh.
vs: Stutter / Stop-Stutter repeats or steps whole frames as a temporal rhythm. Datamosh destroys the picture between frames.
Altered State is perceptual and photographic. Chromatic Aberration is optical color fringing.
Datamosh is codec wreckage, not a general noise overlay.
examples_film: Chairlift's Evident Utensil is a well-known datamosh music video: GOP collapse as the picture. Other music videos adopted the same inter-frame smear.
Features rarely hold it long because it destroys coverage.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: stutter, long-shutter smear, or RGB split. Tell: clean frame repeats, photochemical motion blur, or three colored copies of the subject.
Fix: blocky temporal bleed across a cut, leftover pixels from the previous picture, no new I-frame.

faq.q: What is datamosh in film?
faq.a: Deliberate video-codec collapse. Without a fresh keyframe, motion vectors smear the last valid picture into the next, producing inter-frame wreckage.

faq.q: Datamosh vs stutter
faq.a: Stutter repeats or steps complete frames. Datamosh lets predicted frames destroy the image. One is a rhythm of whole pictures. The other is a melt between them.

faq.q: When should I use datamosh?
faq.a: When the file should fail as the point: music video, corrupted feed, a digital breakdown. Do not use it as a substitute for optical smear or a simple jump cut.

faq.q: How do I prompt datamosh for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for inter-frame collapse, GOP smear, codec wreckage across a cut. Forbid shutter blur, RGB channel split, and freeze-frame stutter unless those are extra.

title: Deep Focus
narrative: A hand stamps a form near the lens. A visitor waits in a distant doorway.
Both are readable. The audience may look at either without a pull or a cut dictating the choice.
Cause and effect share the room. Use it when the story is the whole space: a child outside a window while adults sign papers, a street and a face, two rooms through a doorway.
Staging does the directing. The lens declines to choose.

It is the wrong tool for intimacy that should exclude the world, or when light cannot support a small aperture. Two sharp planes with a blur belt between them are a split diopter or a composite, not deep focus.
how: Balance shorter focal length, smaller aperture, enough illumination, and subject distances that the stop can cover. Some famous deep-focus-looking shots also used in-camera composites.
The screen result does not prove a single-pass method. Prompt: everything sharp from a named near object to the far plane, no rack, no seam, continuous space.
when: A clerk's hand in the near field and an anxious visitor in a far doorway, both sharp, locked wide. Do not claim deep focus if a blur boundary splits the frame in two.
vs: Shallow Focus isolates one plane. Deep focus refuses that isolation.
Split Diopter cheats two sharp distances with a visible or hidden seam and a soft belt. Layered Depth is compositional stacking.
It can be shot shallow or deep. Rack Focus would choose for the audience.
Deep focus leaves the choice open. Forced Perspective may need deep focus so the scale lie is not exposed by blur.
examples_film: Citizen Kane keeps young Kane readable outside the window behind the adults. Touch of Evil holds near and distant figures in the same legible compositions.
The Best Years of Our Lives uses deep space so a whole room can act at once.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: split diopter or a composite of two sharp layers with mush in the middle. Tell: a vertical blur stripe, mismatched grain between planes, or a rack hiding in the still.
Fix: one continuous volume, matched perspective, both distances sharp without a join.

faq.q: What is deep focus in film?
faq.a: A large range of distances appearing acceptably sharp in one image, so near and far action can be read together without a focus pull.

faq.q: Deep focus vs split diopter
faq.a: Deep focus is continuous sharpness through space. A split diopter is a half-lens that sharpens two planes and leaves a blur seam between them.

faq.q: When should I use deep focus?
faq.a: When the audience should find the story in the whole room. Do not use it when isolation is the point, or when the stop would underexpose the set.

faq.q: How do I prompt deep focus for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name a near object and a far plane, require both sharp, forbid rack focus and a split seam, and keep perspective continuous.

title: Diorama
narrative: A city, a ship, a hotel wing sits on a table or a stage, built at an inch to the foot or another ratio. The camera treats it as full size: enough stop for deep focus, a slow pass, fine windows, hard distant key.
Water, fire, and smoke are the hard parts, because fluids do not scale. Use it when a world should be tactile and built: a spacecraft, an industrial skyline, a storybook hotel.

The pleasure is that light is true on small surfaces. It is the wrong tool when you point a tilt-shift lens at a real city to make it look like a model, or when you align two live actors at different distances to lie about size.
Those are cousins. If depth of field is a thin band, the miniature will look like a miniature.
how: Build surface scale (panel lines, dirt, tiny lights). Light with a hard, distant key as if the sun were far.
Stop down. Move slowly.
For water and fire, high-speed capture can help scale. Prompt: miniature world photographed as full size, deep enough focus, tactile model surfaces, not tilt-shift toy blur.
when: An orbital freighter as a detailed model, slow camera pass, tiny windows, deep focus against a black field. Do not add a thin horizontal band of focus that announces tabletop scale.
vs: Tilt-Shift tilts the plane of focus to make a real landscape look like a toy. Diorama is an actual model, usually shot deep to hide scale.
Forced Perspective uses live people and scaled set pieces from one viewpoint. Macro is close focus on small things as small things.
Diorama wants the small thing to read as large.
examples_film: Blade Runner uses industrial miniatures for city and architecture. 2001: A Space Odyssey photographs spacecraft and stations as models.
The Grand Budapest Hotel uses storybook miniatures as a designed world. Those are model stages, not tilt-shift streets.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: tilt-shift, or a digital city with shallow tabletop focus. Tell: a thin focus band, fast toy-like motion, coarse textures, fluids that look like pouring on a desk.
Fix: finer detail, deeper stop, slower move, scale-aware effects.

faq.q: What is diorama in film?
faq.a: Photography of scale models standing in for large objects or places. Real light on real miniature surfaces, sold as full size by focus, speed, and texture.

faq.q: Diorama vs tilt-shift
faq.a: Diorama is a real model, usually shot with enough depth of field to look large. Tilt-shift is a focus trick that makes a real full-size scene look small.

faq.q: When should I use diorama?
faq.a: When a world should be a built, tactile miniature. Do not use it if you only want a toy look on a real city, or a live-action size lie between two actors.

faq.q: How do I prompt diorama for AI image or video?
faq.a: Specify a physical miniature, fine surface scale, deep focus, slow camera. Forbid tilt-shift shallow bands and fast toy acceleration.

title: Distortions
narrative: Walls lean. Faces balloon as they near the glass.
A hallway breathes. Space is not trustworthy.

The cause can be a very wide spherical, a fisheye, anamorphic mumps, heat shimmer, or a shot through a glass of water. Use it when the location should feel unsafe or subjective: a droogs' wide, a binge, a peephole, a fever.
Pick a distortion family and keep it consistent with the glass. It is the wrong tool for a clean normal-lens master, for flare without warp, or for a kaleidoscope of mirrors.
If color fringes without bent lines, that is chromatic aberration. If the whole mind is unhooked, consider altered state, of which distortion may be one part.
how: Choose the glass: 14 mm or fisheye for barrel, long glass for pincushion, anamorphic for mumps and wave, a close diopter for melt at the edge. Get too close to faces on a wide and perspective distortion adds to optical distortion.
Prompt: optical distortion around [Subject], stretched edges, melted geometry, named wide or fisheye, not a flare overlay.
when: A close wide on a face in a tense interior, edges stretching, the room bowing, space untrustworthy. Do not keep a 50 mm rectilinear room and paste melted corners as a sticker.
vs: Fisheye is the extreme barrel member of this family, with a circular or strongly bowed field. Lens Flare is scatter, not geometry.
Chromatic Aberration fringes color on edges. 14mm Ultra-Wide distorts through field of view and proximity even when the designer corrects barrel.
Altered State may include distortion plus time and color.
examples_film: A Clockwork Orange uses extreme wides so rooms and faces are geometrically hostile. Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas melts space as intoxication.
Those are glass and proximity, not a warp filter parked on a normal lens.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: lens flare, fisheye circular crop without the scene, or altered-state color smear with straight walls. Tell: rainbow streaks, a round porthole sticker, or a clean rectilinear room with a melted overlay.
Fix: choose a lens family, bow lines, let near faces balloon, keep the warp attached to the optic.

faq.q: What is lens distortion in film?
faq.a: Geometric warping of space by the optic or by shooting through a distorting surface. Straight lines bow or stretch. The map of the room is no longer true.

faq.q: Distortions vs fisheye
faq.a: Fisheye is a specific extreme barrel lens. Distortions is the larger family: barrel, pincushion, anamorphic wave, heat, glass of water. Fisheye is one tool in that kit.

faq.q: When should I use distortions?
faq.a: When space should not be trustworthy. Do not use them on coverage that still has to be architecturally honest.

faq.q: How do I prompt distortions for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the glass (ultra-wide, fisheye) or the surface, describe bowed lines and stretched edges, and forbid flare-only artifacts or a sticker warp.

title: Double Exposure
narrative: A face in a city. A ghost in rain.
Fireplace flames laid over a locked interior. Two times share density.

The result can be lyrical (memory, a second self) or purely practical (an element you could not shoot with the first pass). Use it when two records should coexist: a thought over a room, a spirit over a landscape, fire added later.
Superimposition is the family. Actor doubling with a split matte is one application, not the whole technique.
It is the wrong tool when you need two solid bodies that occlude each other, cast contact shadows, and pass objects. That is duplication or a split-matte composite, not a ghosted overlay.
It is also the wrong tool when a dissolve would carry you from one time to the next instead of stacking them.
how: In camera: expose, matte off part of the gate or shoot a full overlay, rewind, expose again with matched lighting. Optically: bi-pack or printer pass.
Digitally: additive mix or screened layers, or a hard split matte for twins. Lock the camera unless both passes share motion control.
Prompt two named images sharing one frame, optical overlay, not a hard cut and not a morph.
when: A face superimposed over rain-soaked rooftops so memory and place occupy one still. Do not use a translucent overlay when two twins must sit at one table and pour tea.
vs: Dissolve is a temporal crossfade from shot A to shot B. Double exposure holds both at once.
Duplication makes two solid performances of the same body in one space, usually with mattes, not ghosts. Morph interpolates geometry from one form into another.
Overlay is not transformation. Match Cut joins two shots.
Double exposure never cuts.
examples_film: Persona stacks faces until identity is a density problem. The Tree of Life lays memory over photographed nature.
The Shining adds fireplace flames with a separate exposure. The Parent Trap and Adaptation use related splitting and doubling when two bodies must coexist, which is the cousin, not the same overlay.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: dissolve, morph, or twin duplication. Tell: one image simply fades into the next, or two solid people with no shared density, or a face melting into a building.
Fix: keep both images present, set opacity or a matte on purpose, and decide whether the second pass is ghost or solid.

faq.q: What is double exposure in film?
faq.a: Two image records combined on one frame, in camera, in an optical printer, or digitally. Elements shot at different times appear together.

faq.q: Double exposure vs dissolve
faq.a: A dissolve is a transition that leaves shot A for shot B. A double exposure is a stack: both pictures remain visible in the same frame.

faq.q: When should I use double exposure?
faq.a: When two times, two selves, or two elements should occupy one image. Do not use it when you need two solid, occluding bodies.

faq.q: How do I prompt double exposure for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name both images, say optical overlay or in-camera double exposure, and specify whether the second pass is translucent or matted. Ban morph and hard split-screen unless that is the job.

title: Duplication
narrative: One person is not a single self. Two performances share a kitchen.
They argue, pass a look, fail to occupy the same chair. Contact shadows, eyelines, and any exchanged object are the hard problems.
Two similar-looking people are not automatically this effect. Use it when identity splits in space: twins, a writer and his brother, a man meeting himself.

The encounter should feel physically ordinary. It is the wrong tool when the second self is a ghost (double exposure), when the frame is simply divided (split-screen as the visible device), or when one body melts into another (morph).
If they cannot sit in depth and occlude, you have the wrong cousin.
how: Lock the camera or repeat the move with motion control. Record a clean plate.
Shoot each performance with matched light. Use a split matte where bodies stay apart, or tracked masks where they overlap.

Plan contact and handed objects as separate shots or as later help. Prompt: the same figure twice in one frame, solid bodies, matched lighting, not a ghost overlay, not a visible split line unless you want split-screen.
when: Two versions of one woman across a kitchen table, distinct posture and clothing, shared shadows, locked camera. Do not stack them as translucent densities, and do not leave a vertical join down the table.
vs: Double Exposure is additive overlay. Ghosts, not two sitters.
Split Screen shows two pictures with a designed border, which can be how duplication is done if the join is visible. Seamless duplication hides the join.
Morph turns one form into another over time. Duplication keeps both.
examples_film: The Parent Trap seats one performer as both twins in shared compositions. Adaptation puts Charlie and Donald in the same scenes.
Enemy multiplies a man as encounter. The Social Network uses similar motion-control doubling for the Winklevoss pair.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: double exposure, split-screen with a hard line, or two lookalikes who are not the same face. Tell: translucent stack, a seam down the set, mismatched grain or key, hovering hands.
Fix: locked or motion-controlled plates, identical identity, shared shadows, planned occlusion.

faq.q: What is duplication in film?
faq.a: The same performer appearing more than once in a shot as solid bodies, usually via split mattes or motion control. It is a spatial double, not a ghost overlay.

faq.q: Duplication vs double exposure
faq.a: Double exposure stacks densities so both images show through. Duplication composites two performances so each body can occlude, sit, and cast shadow.

faq.q: When should I use duplication?
faq.a: When one person must meet themselves as a physical other. Do not use it for a memory ghost or for a morph from one face into another.

faq.q: How do I prompt duplication for AI image or video?
faq.a: Ask for the same face twice, distinct poses, matched lighting, contact shadows, locked camera. Forbid translucent overlay and a visible split line unless split-screen is the point.

title: Echo Print
narrative: Use it when a gesture has already happened and the present cannot shake it. A head turns and the old profile hangs a few pixels away.
A step leaves a faint body where the foot was. Time reads as a registration error.
It is the wrong tool for a clean double of two living people in conversation. If both images are fully exposed and equally sharp, you shot a superimposition, not a stain.
how: Keep the camera locked or on a short path. Copy the previous frame, offset it along the motion vector by a few pixels or a few milliseconds, and print it at lower opacity.
Optical printers did this with a slight mis-register. Video echo does it with delay.
One key still lights the live body. The ghost has no second key.
Prompt an afterimage offset in time or register, and say that the last frame is still printed on this one.
when: Use it for the beat after a look, a blow, or a departure, when the last pose should remain as a stain. Do not use it to introduce a twin who must occupy the room as a solid person.
vs: Double Exposure combines two complete pictures. An echo print is a faded offset of the same action.
Step Printing repeats discrete frames to slow or stutter a take. The echo is a smear of register, not a held frame.
examples_film: Experimental optical printing and title-design ghosts are the grammar: a credit or a figure that leaves a trail of itself. Video-echo music videos do the same with delay.
These are uses of the stain, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Double Exposure . The tell is two equally solid bodies, both keyed, both sharp.
The fix is one live subject and a fainter, offset copy of the same pose, no second lamp.

faq.q: What is echo print in film?
faq.a: Echo print leaves a ghosted afterimage offset in time or register, as if the last frame were still printed on this one. The past of the gesture remains visible as a stain.

faq.q: Echo print vs double exposure
faq.a: Double exposure combines two complete images. Echo print reprints a delayed or mis-registered copy of the same action at lower strength. One is two pictures. The other is a trail.

faq.q: When should I use echo print?
faq.a: Use it when a movement should leave a mark: a turn, a blow, a person already gone. Skip it when you need two solid people sharing a scene.

faq.q: How do I prompt echo print for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name the subject, then demand a ghosted afterimage offset in time or register. Keep one key. Say the last frame is still printed on this one. For video, afterimages should trail the present pose.

title: Feedback
narrative: The medium stares at itself. A face on a tube is recaptured, recaptured again, and the room becomes a hallway of the same look.
Use it when the story is about watching, broadcast, or a mind that cannot get out of the signal. It is the wrong tool for a simple loop of action.
If the last frame merely sews to the first, you have a cycle in time, not a camera eating its monitor.
how: Aim the taking lens at a playback screen that shows the live feed. A slight off-axis angle builds a corridor.
Dead-on nesting builds rectangles inside rectangles. Gain, lag, and the phosphor or pixel bloom set how fast the tunnel eats itself.
The subject is usually close to the screen so the first generation is readable. Prompt video feedback around the subject: camera looking into its own output, infinite corridor of the same face.
when: Use it when a person is trapped in a transmission, a title, or a night of monitors. Do not use it as wallpaper behind a dialogue scene that still needs geography.
vs: Kaleidoscope mirrors facets of one image into symmetry. Feedback nests generations of the same capture.
Infinite Loop sews the last frame to the first in time. Feedback is optical recursion, not a cycle of action.
examples_film: 1960s tape experiments pointed cameras at monitors until the image tunnelled. The Doctor Who howlaround titles are the famous broadcast version.
Music videos still use the same recursive corridor. Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Kaleidoscope or a simple video loop. The tell is mirrored wedges or a repeating walk with no nested screen.
The fix is a camera aimed at its own output, generations shrinking down a tunnel.

faq.q: What is feedback in film?
faq.a: Video feedback is a camera looking into its own output so the image rephotographs itself into a nested corridor. Bloom, lag, and a tunnel of the same face are the picture.

faq.q: Feedback vs kaleidoscope
faq.a: A kaleidoscope mirrors one image into symmetric facets. Feedback recaptures the live picture from a monitor, stacking generations rather than folding the frame.

faq.q: When should I use feedback?
faq.a: Use it when the story is the signal watching itself: broadcast, hypnosis, a face trapped in a tube. Skip it for ordinary looping action.

faq.q: How do I prompt feedback for AI image or video?
faq.a: Say video feedback, camera looking into its own output, infinite corridor of the same face. For motion, the image should eat itself into a tunnel. Keep a readable first generation.

title: Film Grain
narrative: The image is made of particles that change every frame. Shadows crawl.
Midtones have a living grain. Highlights are not a separate smooth plate.
Format and stock speed set the size: 16mm reads coarser in the frame than 35mm or 65mm. Use it when the picture should feel exposed and processed, not drawn.
A rooftop at blue hour, a winter platform, a handheld interior. Grain should scale with density, not stamp the same speckle on sky and coat alike.
It is the wrong tool as a default film look on a sharp digital plate. If the grain is identical on every frame, or floats above motion blur, it is a layer, not an emulsion.
how: On film, choose stock and format: faster stocks and smaller negatives show more grain. Push processing increases it.
Digitally, generate monochromatic grain that is denser in midtones and shadows, temporally unstable, and finer on larger implied formats. Do not sharpen after.
Prompt 16mm or 35mm texture, living grain, no overlay.
when: A charcoal coat on wet slate at blue hour, 35mm grain in the dusk, chimney smoke breaking into particles. Do not paste coarse grain on an already sharp product still and call it developed.
vs: Halation is highlight bloom in the layers, not the particle field. Filmic Faded is a contrast and color decision (lifted blacks, reduced saturation), which can sit with grain but is not grain.
Light Leak fogs from the edge with unfiltered light. Grain is the stock's texture everywhere the image has density.
examples_film: The Revenant lets natural-light textures read as a developed image rather than a clean sensor. Roma is large-format stillness with a photochemical finish, not a grain storm.
Saving Private Ryan uses a harsher, tighter grain as combat stock language.
mistakes: Wrong cousin: a repeating overlay, digital noise, or halation bloom. Tell: identical grain on every frame, speckle in clipped whites, or a wallpaper that ignores motion.
Fix: per-frame grain, format-sized particles, density-weighted, no overlay.

faq.q: What is film grain in film?
faq.a: Random texture from silver crystals or dye clouds in the emulsion. Size follows stock speed and negative area. It changes every frame.

faq.q: Film grain vs halation
faq.a: Grain is the particle structure of the image. Halation is a warm glow around bright highlights from light bouncing in the film layers.

faq.q: When should I use film grain?
faq.a: When the image should feel developed rather than rendered. Match grain size to format. Do not stamp one overlay on every shot.

faq.q: How do I prompt film grain for AI image or video?
faq.a: Name 16mm or 35mm, ask for living per-frame texture in shadows and midtones, and forbid a repeating overlay.

title: Floating Fall
narrative: Someone has left the roof. The coat opens late.
Hair hangs. The street is still far.
Use it for the beat after the push, when the drop should feel like a hymn and a disaster at once. It is the wrong tool for a hover, and for a real-time camera drop.
If there is no net descent, you shot levitation. If the whole frame is simply overcranked equally, you shot slow motion of a normal fall.
how: Keep downward travel. Delay gravity on hair, coat, and debris more than on the torso.
If the camera is locked, the body drifts down through a stable frame. If the camera also drops, the building or cliff should still parallax as falling-past.
A side-key keeps the body separate from the void. Name the height and what is already below.
Prompt a floating fall: a body hanging in slow drop, delayed gravity. For video, falls in slow, floating pieces, delayed gravity.
when: Use it for the second after leaving the ledge, the dream of dropping, the stunt that should hang. Do not use it for a slapstick trip down stairs unless the joke is that time went soft.
vs: Levitation hovers with no net drop. Falling uses real-time weight, ground rushing.
Slow Motion overcranks the whole shot equally. A floating fall delays gravity on the body while descent remains the plot.
examples_film: Inception 's hallway physics turns a fall into a drift through architecture. The Matrix rooftop and street drops hang bodies in delayed time.
Grammar of delayed gravity, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousins are balloon Levitation and ordinary Slow Motion . The tell is a body that never descends, or a normal fall that is only slowed.
The fix is net downward travel, delayed cloth, and a readable ground.

faq.q: What is floating fall in film?
faq.a: A floating fall is a drop with delayed gravity: the body hangs in a slow descent, hair and coat late, the ground still far. It is a fall, not a hover.

faq.q: Floating fall vs levitation
faq.a: Levitation stays up. A floating fall goes down with the clock wrong. One needs a gap under the feet that does not close. The other needs a ground that is coming.

faq.q: When should I use floating fall?
faq.a: Use it for the beat after the push, when a drop should hang. Skip it for a true hover, and for a real-time camera fall with rushing ground.

faq.q: How do I prompt floating fall for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Floating fall of [Subject], a body hanging in slow drop, hair and coat in delayed gravity. Name height and ground. For video, slow floating pieces, path still down.
